Run the compact vacuum with the brush attachment along the back wall and the top board, then follow with a barely-damp microfiber cloth and neutral pH multi-surface cleaner. Dry it off before you move down.

surfaces.surface: Each shelf board, fully cleared
surfaces.method: Take everything off the board rather than wiping around it. Vacuum the loose flour and grain dust first, then wipe with a cloth wrung out in neutral pH cleaner. Change to a dry cloth and take the board fully dry, because a damp board plus grain dust is what starts a pantry smelling.

surfaces.surface: The front lip and shelf edge
surfaces.method: Flour dust drifts forward and settles along the front lip where you never look. Vacuum it, then wipe the edge and the underside of the lip with a damp cloth and dry it, since this is the line hands brush every time they reach in.

surfaces.surface: The containers, lids, and scoops
surfaces.method: Wipe each canister and jar on the outside with a damp cloth, paying attention to the lid seal and the pour spout where fine dust cakes. Wash any scoop that lives in the grain in warm soapy water and dry it fully before it goes back in.

surfaces.surface: The back corners and the seam where board meets upright
surfaces.method: Fine dust packs into the back corners and the seam. Use the vacuum crevice tool or a dry detail brush to lift it out, then wipe. A dry cloth or brush first every time, because a wet cloth just turns flour to paste in the corner.

surfaces.surface: The floor beneath the bottom shelf
surfaces.method: Vacuum the floor under the lowest board where spilled grains roll and gather. Wipe it with a damp cloth last, once the shelves above are done and dry, and take it dry so nothing tracks back up.

inspect_as_you_clean: A chewed corner on a bag or paper packet, or small dark droppings in a back corner, both signs something is getting in and worth flagging.
Fine webbing, tiny moths, or clumping in an opened grain, the look of pantry pests that spread from one bag to the whole shelf.
A container lid that no longer clicks or seals, so the contents are quietly going stale.
A shelf board that has started to bow in the middle under the weight sitting on it.
A damp patch or a musty note at the back wall, or spots of rust on a wire shelf, telling you moisture is coming from behind.

zones.time_note: most of it in Sort, since the work is turning cans to read dates and counting duplicates
zones.purpose: Holds the cans and jars that turn an empty-fridge week into dinner.
zones.done_looks_like: Cans sit in rows on risers with every label facing you: tomatoes together, beans together, soup together. No dented seams, no domed lids, no jar hidden behind another jar, and the oldest date in each row standing at the front of it.

passes.sort: Take every can and jar out, turn each one until you find the date, and put the dented, rusted and bulging ones straight into the bin rather than back on the shelf. Then count duplicates, because four jars of the same pasta sauce is telling you exactly what you keep buying blind.
passes.straighten: Rows by meal rather than by size. Tomatoes, coconut milk and stock together because they cook together, beans and tuna together because they are lunch, and tall jars behind short cans so nothing disappears.
passes.shine: Wipe the sticky rings where a honey jar or a sauce lid has wept, and wash the threads of the jars you open most. A sticky shelf edge is how ants find their way to you.
passes.safety: Poison, choke, or strangle: a can with a domed lid, a weeping seam, or a hiss as it opens is spoiled rather than merely old. It does not get tasted, decanted, or given to the dog. "Find it, and fix it now."
passes.standardize: Label each row with its category and put the back row up on a riser so it sits above the front row. Once you can read every label without moving a can, the gap where the chopped tomatoes used to be is your shopping list writing itself.
passes.sustain: When you sit down to write the shopping list, walk the can rows first and read the gaps. A missing tin of tomatoes is far easier to see on a shelf than to remember at a table.

the_call.title: The best-before you keep arguing with
the_call.text: The soup two years past its date, the chickpeas whose date has rubbed off, the fancy jar somebody gave you that you are saving for an occasion that has not arrived. Best-before is about quality rather than safety, so you have been keeping these on a technicality and never eating them. End the argument with one pass: anything past best-before goes into a meal in the next seven days or it goes out this week. Anything past a use-by date goes now. Anything dented on the seam, rusted, or domed goes now regardless of the date, and it does not go to the food bank either. If you would not open it tonight, you are not saving it, you are storing it.

watch_for.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
watch_for.text: A bulging or leaking can is a spoilage warning and no amount of cooking makes it safe. Bag it sealed, bin it, and wash the shelf underneath where it stood.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: A dense row of cans on a high shelf. One tin landing on a bare foot is a broken toe, and a glass sauce jar bursting on tile leaves splinters you find for weeks. Cans and glass belong below shoulder height.

leave_behind.standard: Every label faces out, every row holds one category, and the oldest date sits at the front of its row.
leave_behind.trigger: When you carry the recycling out past the pantry, you face up the can rows on the way.

shine_detail.shine_summary: The sticky ring is what you are hunting. Wipe every weeping lid and the shelf under it, wash the threads of the jars you open most, and leave no tacky edge for ants to follow.

surfaces.surface: The shelf boards and the riser tiers
surfaces.method: Lift the cans and jars off in rows and vacuum the loose dust, then wipe the board and each step riser with a cloth wrung out in neutral pH cleaner. Dry it so labels do not sit on a damp surface and lift.

surfaces.surface: The sticky rings where a jar has wept
surfaces.method: Find the tacky rings under honey, syrup, and sauce jars and work them with a warm damp cloth and neutral pH cleaner until the shelf squeaks clean. A sticky edge left behind is exactly how ants find their way to the row.

surfaces.surface: The jar threads and lids
surfaces.method: For the jars you open most, wipe the threads and the underside of the lid where dried drips build. A dry detail brush gets into the thread grooves before you finish with a damp cloth.

surfaces.surface: The can exteriors and rims
surfaces.method: Wipe the tops and rims of cans as they come off, where kitchen dust settles into a greasy film. Set them back label-out with the oldest date at the front of the row.

surfaces.surface: The shelf front edge and the back of the shelf
surfaces.method: Run a damp cloth along the front edge hands brush past, then reach to the back board behind the rear row, which only gets cleared on a full empty-out. Vacuum first, wipe second, dry last.

surfaces.surface: The floor beneath the bottom shelf
surfaces.method: Vacuum the floor under the lowest row where a rolled can or a dried syrup drip ends up, then wipe with a damp cloth and dry it, working after the shelves above are done.

inspect_as_you_clean: A domed or bulging lid, a weeping seam, or a can that hisses, all of which say spoiled rather than merely old, worth flagging before it is opened.
A rust ring on the base of a can or on the shelf under it, a sign of a slow moisture problem where the tin has stood.
A fresh sticky drip pointing to a jar that has cracked or a lid that has failed and is leaking now.
An ant trail or a single scout following a sugary edge, telling you a sticky spot got missed last time.
A shelf board bowing under a dense row of cans, or a label peeling with damp behind it.

zones.time_note: most of it in Sort, testing leaveners and deciding about the decorating gear
zones.purpose: Holds everything you need to start a bake without a trip to the shop first.
zones.done_looks_like: Flour, sugar and brown sugar in sealed containers you can open one-handed. Baking powder, bicarbonate of soda and yeast together in one small box with their dates showing. Cutters, cases and piping tips in a single lift-out bin, and no loose sprinkles rolling around the shelf.

passes.sort: Test the leaveners rather than guessing: a spoon of baking powder into hot water should fizz hard, and yeast in warm sugared water should foam. The dead ones go, along with the brick of hardened brown sugar and the cocoa that has turned grey.
passes.straighten: Build one lift-out bin holding flour, sugar, bicarb, vanilla and a scoop, so starting a bake is one trip to the shelf instead of six. Cutters and piping tips live in a second bin behind it, because they are the end of a bake and never the beginning.
passes.shine: Flour turns to paste under a damp cloth, so brush or vacuum the shelf dry first and wipe afterwards. Wash the scoop rather than burying it back in the flour between bakes.
passes.safety: Poison, choke, or strangle: almond meal, nut flours and sesame share this shelf with everything else, and one shared scoop carries traces straight into a birthday cake. Give each allergen its own sealed container and its own scoop, and stand it at the end of the row where nobody grabs it by mistake.
passes.standardize: Write the opening date on the lid of every leavener the day you open it, because the printed date stops meaning much once air is in the tin. The bin sits in the same spot with the same contents, so a missing scoop or an absent vanilla shows before the butter is out.
passes.sustain: When the oven timer goes and the bake comes out to cool, the bin goes back to its shelf with the scoop washed and the flour topped up.

the_call.title: The kit for the baker you meant to become
the_call.text: The piping set from the birthday you decorated once, the fondant, the third tart tin, the specialty flour from a month of enthusiastic bread. This is the hardest shelf in the pantry, because letting it go feels like admitting something about yourself. Here is the rule that settles it: keep the tools for what you have baked twice, and let go of the tools for what you have baked once. Twice means it is a thing you do. Once means it was a good afternoon, and the afternoon has already happened. Whatever survives that test earns its bin space. The rest goes to somebody who bakes this month, not into a box in the garage where you will meet it again in three years.

watch_for.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
watch_for.text: Cross-contact between nut flours and everything else on the shelf, plus small decorating pieces like silver balls and mini cutters sitting on a low shelf within a toddler's reach.

watch_for.question: Fall
watch_for.text: Spilled flour or sugar on a hard kitchen floor is genuinely slick, and you will be walking a hot tray across it. Sweep the spill when it happens rather than when the bake is done.

leave_behind.standard: One lift-out baking bin with a washed scoop, leaveners dated on the lid the day they are opened, and allergen flours sealed with a scoop of their own.
leave_behind.trigger: When you set the oven to preheat, you check the leavener dates while it comes up to temperature.

shine_detail.shine_summary: Flour turns to paste the instant a wet cloth touches it, so this zone is dry-first, always. Brush or vacuum the shelf clean, wipe afterwards, and wash the scoop instead of burying it back in the flour.

surfaces.surface: The shelf board under the flour and sugar
surfaces.method: Brush or vacuum the loose flour off the board completely while it is dry, then and only then wipe with a barely-damp cloth and neutral pH cleaner. Wetting flour first just smears it into a grey skin you have to scrape.

surfaces.surface: The flour, sugar, and brown-sugar containers
surfaces.method: Wipe each container on the outside, and pay attention to the one-handed lid mechanism where a dusting of flour stops it clicking shut. Dry the rim so no damp gets trapped under the seal.

surfaces.surface: The scoop
surfaces.method: Wash the scoop in warm soapy water and dry it fully rather than pushing it back into the flour between bakes, where a damp scoop seeds a hard clump.

surfaces.surface: The lift-out bin of cutters, cases, and piping tips
surfaces.method: Tip the bin out, vacuum the crumbs and stray sprinkles from its corners, and wipe it dry. Check that each cutter and tip is dry before it goes back so they do not spot with rust.

surfaces.surface: The allergen containers at the end of the row
surfaces.method: Wipe the sealed nut-flour and sesame containers on the outside with their own cloth, and wash their dedicated scoops separately in warm soapy water so no trace travels back down the shelf.

surfaces.surface: The floor directly below
surfaces.method: Sweep or vacuum any spilled flour or sugar off the floor as you go, since it is genuinely slick underfoot and you will be walking a hot tray across it.

inspect_as_you_clean: Tiny beetles or weevils in an opened flour, or fine webbing across the surface, the sign a bag has turned and needs flagging before it spreads.
Sugar or flour that has clumped hard, telling you damp is getting into a container whose seal has gone.
A one-handed lid that no longer clicks shut, so the contents are open to the air and to pests.
A hairline crack in a plastic canister, or a cutter or tip showing the first orange bloom of rust.
An allergen container sharing a scoop with the open shelf, a cross-contact risk worth calling out on the spot.

zones.time_note: most of it in Straighten, because the fix here is height and containers rather than volume
zones.purpose: Holds what goes into a lunchbox, and what a child is allowed to take without asking.
zones.done_looks_like: One open bin at child height holding only snacks you have already said yes to, and a higher shelf holding the ones that need an adult. Every reusable container has its own lid sitting on it, and the number of containers matches the number of lunches you genuinely pack.

passes.sort: Match every lid to a container and bin the orphans in both directions, the lidless tubs and the lids for tubs that died. Then pull the snack boxes with two bars rattling in the bottom, combine them, and flatten the empty cartons.
passes.straighten: Pre-approved snacks go into an open bin the child can reach without a stool. The ones that start an argument go on the shelf above their eye line. Lunch bags and ice packs stand next to the containers rather than in a drawer in another room.
passes.shine: Empty the bin and wipe it out, because crushed crackers and dried fruit-pouch drips collect in the bottom corners. Check every lunch bag for the sandwich nobody mentioned, and wash the liners.
passes.safety: Poison, choke, or strangle: whole nuts, hard sweets and grapes go straight from an open bin into a small mouth. Set the bin's contents by the youngest person in the house who can reach it, and think about a classmate's allergy before a nut bar goes into a shared lunch hall.
passes.standardize: The bin is the rule made visible. What is in it is allowed, what is not in it needs asking, and a photo taped inside the pantry door shows what a properly stocked bin looks like.
passes.sustain: When the lunchboxes come out in the evening, lids go back onto their containers and the bin gets topped up for the morning before anybody sits down.

the_call.title: Whether the answer is yours or the bin's
the_call.text: You are negotiating snacks several times a day, and every one of those is a fresh decision made while you are busy and being asked twice. The call is to move the decision off the moment and onto the shelf. Choose once, in daylight and not at four o'clock, exactly what a child may take without asking, and put precisely that in the open bin at their height. Everything else goes above eye line and requires you. Then hold the line: when the bin is empty at four o'clock, the answer is that the bin is empty, not that you will go and find something. That single refusal is what makes the bin real. Until you hold it, the bin is decoration and you are still the one being asked.

watch_for.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
watch_for.text: Hard sweets, whole nuts and small round cheeses in an open bin a two-year-old can reach. The bin's contents are set by the youngest child in the house, not the oldest.

watch_for.question: Fall
watch_for.text: A child climbing the shelving to reach the higher snack shelf. If it is worth climbing for, either move it out of the pantry entirely or fix the shelving unit to the wall.

leave_behind.standard: The open bin at child height holds only pre-approved snacks and is refilled to one marked level, and no container returns to the shelf without its lid on it.
leave_behind.trigger: When the lunchboxes are emptied at the sink after school, the bin gets filled back to its line before the bags go on their hook.

shine_detail.shine_summary: The mess here hides in the bottom corners of the bin and in a lunch bag nobody emptied. Tip the bin out, wipe the drips clean, and check every bag for the sandwich no one mentioned.

surfaces.surface: The higher adult-controlled shelf
surfaces.method: Work top down. Clear the higher shelf, vacuum any crumbs, and wipe the board with a damp cloth and neutral pH cleaner before you drop to the child-height bin.

surfaces.surface: The low child-height snack bin
surfaces.method: Empty the bin completely and wipe it out, getting right into the bottom corners where crushed crackers and dried fruit-pouch drips collect. Dry it before the snacks go back.

surfaces.surface: The reusable containers and their lids
surfaces.method: Match each container to its lid as you wipe them, washing out in warm soapy water any that held a leaking snack. Set aside a lid that is missing or warped rather than stacking it back.

surfaces.surface: The reusable drink bottles and their spouts
surfaces.method: Wash each bottle in warm soapy water and run the bottle brush down inside, then work the spout, straw, and screw threads where a sour film hides in the seam. Dry them fully upside down and open before they go back.

surfaces.surface: The lunch bags and their liners
surfaces.method: Turn every lunch bag inside out, shake the crumbs into the bin, and wash the liners in warm soapy water. Dry them fully open so nothing goes back damp and sour.

surfaces.surface: The bin exterior and the shelf edge
surfaces.method: Wipe the outside of the bin and the shelf front where sticky hands land, then run a damp cloth along the shelf board underneath. Dry it so no sugary film is left to draw ants.

inspect_as_you_clean: A forgotten sandwich or a piece of fruit going off in the bottom of a lunch bag, worth flagging the moment you find it.
Soft mould spotting inside a drink bottle or in the seam of a fruit-pouch drip left too long.
A container lid that has split or warped so it no longer seals, letting the snack go stale or leak.
The shelving unit rocking or its wall anchor working loose where a child has been climbing to the higher shelf.
A sticky sugary drip at the back of the bin that a scout ant has already found.

zones.time_note: most of it in Sort and in the lifting, since bulk packs are heavy and each one needs dating before it goes back
zones.purpose: Holds the reserve that feeds the working shelves, and nothing else.
zones.done_looks_like: Sacks of rice, cases of tinned tomatoes and packs of kitchen roll, each written on with the month it arrived, all standing at or below waist height. A maximum number written on the shelf edge for each line, and the count on the shelf sitting at or under it. Nothing stacked in front of anything else.

passes.sort: Open up the back of this zone and meet what you forgot you owned: the second sack of rice, the twelve-pack of a sauce nobody liked, the case of sparkling water from a party in another season. Anything you hold more than one spare of moves forward into the working shelves this month or it leaves.
passes.straighten: Weight decides height. Sacks and cases go on the floor or the bottom shelf on a board, kitchen roll and paper napkins go up top because they are light, and everything sits one row deep so you never move a case to see a case.
passes.shine: Sweep the floor of this zone and check the underside of the bottom case for damp, where a concrete floor or an outside wall is sweating. Cardboard that has gone soft is warning you about moisture before your food does.
passes.safety: Fall, cut, or crush: a stacked column of cases is stable right up until somebody pulls the second one from the bottom. Stack no higher than your chest, bend at the knees for the rice sack, and never store a heavy case overhead where getting it down means catching it.
passes.standardize: Write a maximum for each line on the shelf edge, two of this, one of that, and mark every pack with its arrival month as it goes in. Undated bulk is where the saving quietly expires out of sight.
passes.sustain: When a working container out in the pantry runs empty, you pull its replacement from the front of backstock and add the item to the list on the same trip. The gap on the shelf is the whole signal.

the_call.title: The warehouse pack that was not a saving
the_call.text: You bought the big one because the unit price was better, and some of it went stale, rancid, or simply boring before you reached the bottom. The honest question is not whether the price was good. It is whether you have ever finished one of these in time. So write down, for each item, the largest quantity you have genuinely used up before it turned, and make that number your maximum on the shelf edge. Until your count falls back below that number you do not buy the item again, whatever the shelf price is doing. Anything already over the line goes forward into meals this month or out to a food bank while it is still in date. A cupboard full of food you will not eat is not a store of value, it is money you have already spent.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: Cases stacked above chest height, and a heavy rice sack lifted off the floor with a twist in your back. Stack low, and slide the sack out onto a step or a chair before you lift it properly.

watch_for.question: Fall
watch_for.text: A floor-stacked case left near the doorway of a dim pantry is a shin-height trip in the dark. Keep the floor inside the door clear and put a light where your hand reaches it before your foot does.

leave_behind.standard: Every pack carries its arrival month, every line has a maximum written on the shelf edge, and stock is always pulled from the front.
leave_behind.trigger: When you get home from a big shop, you write the month on each pack with the marker that lives on that shelf, before anything gets put away.

zones.chapter_ref: See Chapter 24, the checklist and schedule.

shine_detail.shine_summary: This is a floor-and-underside zone. Sweep the floor, lift and check the bottom case for damp, and read the cardboard, because soft board warns you about moisture long before your food shows it.

surfaces.surface: The shelf edges carrying the max-count labels
surfaces.method: Wipe the shelf edges and the written count labels with a barely-damp cloth so the numbers stay readable from the doorway. Dry them so the ink does not run or the label lift.

surfaces.surface: The cases and sacks themselves
surfaces.method: Wipe down the outside of each case and the sacks of rice or flour, taking dust off the tops where it settles thickest. Set them back with the arrival month still facing out.

surfaces.surface: The underside of the bottom case
surfaces.method: Lift the lowest case and feel the underside and the board beneath it for damp. This is the spot a concrete floor or an outside wall sweats into, so it is the first place to look every time.

surfaces.surface: The floor of the zone
surfaces.method: Sweep or vacuum the whole floor, working from the back wall out to the door. Wipe any spill with a damp cloth and dry it, since this floor stays out of sight between visits.

surfaces.surface: The back wall and the doorway floor
surfaces.method: Wipe the back wall behind the stack, especially where it meets an outside wall, and clear the floor just inside the doorway so nothing sits at shin height in the dark.

inspect_as_you_clean: Cardboard that has gone soft or dark at the bottom of a case, the moisture warning that arrives before the food spoils.
A water stain, a bloom of mould, or beads of condensation on the back or outside wall.
Droppings or gnawed corners low down, or a chewed sack, telling you something is coming in at floor level.
A sack that has started to bulge, split, or leak its contents onto the shelf below.
A case crushed or bowing under the weight above it, or rust creeping up a metal shelf leg near the damp floor.

rooms.intro: The dining room has one job, and it is the only room in the house that can quietly lose that job without anyone noticing. The table becomes a desk, the sideboard becomes a filing cabinet, and dinner moves to the couch. Start with the table, because a room that can seat everyone tonight is a room worth defending tomorrow.

tips.label: Where to start
tips.text: Start with the Dining Table. It is the quickest zone in the room and the only one whose result shows up at dinner the same evening, which buys you the goodwill to open the sideboard drawers tomorrow.

tips.label: Cleaning note
tips.text: Work top down and begin with the light fixture hanging over the table, since dust falls from it straight onto the surface you eat from. Chair rungs and legs next, tabletop last, and condition bare wood a few times a year so spills bead instead of soaking in.

tips.label: The trap
tips.text: Clearing the table into the sideboard drawers is not clearing. The sideboard quietly absorbs everything the table sheds, which is why its drawers and shelves take far longer to work through than the wood sitting on top of them.

zones.time_note: most of it in Sort, deciding where the homework and the unopened mail actually live
zones.purpose: Seat everyone for a shared meal without having to move anything first.
zones.done_looks_like: One centerpiece on bare wood and nothing else, every chair pushed all the way in with nothing hanging off its back, placemats and trivets in the sideboard drawer one step away, and no paper anywhere on the surface.

passes.sort: Clear the whole table onto the floor in one armful, then sort what came off by owner rather than by type. The homework, the unopened mail, and the half-finished craft project each go back to a person, not back to the table.
passes.straighten: Placemats, trivets, and the napkin basket belong in the nearest sideboard drawer, one step from where you set the table. Anything you find yourself carrying in from the kitchen twice a day is sleeping in the wrong drawer.
passes.shine: Run a fingernail down the leaf seam and the joint where the top meets the pedestal, because that is where crumbs collect and stay. Wipe the chair rungs and the underside lip of the table where hands grip it to pull a chair in.
passes.safety: Lift and rock each chair to find a loose rung or a joint that has started working, and turn any chair that moves to face the wall so nobody sits on it before the joint is glued. Keep a trivet in the table's own drawer so a hot dish never lands on bare wood, and keep tall candles well clear of the runner ends.
passes.standardize: The centerpiece is the table's only permanent resident and its footprint is the boundary. Photograph the table both set and cleared, and tape both pictures inside the sideboard door so the right state is not something anyone has to remember.
passes.sustain: When the plates go to the sink after dinner, the homework, the mail, and the craft box ride along in the same trip. Nothing waits for a second journey.

the_call.title: The person who works at the table
the_call.text: Someone in the house has made the table their desk, and every reset you have run so far has been a polite request that they stop. Requests do not hold. Here is the rule that settles it: if an activity lands on the table more than three evenings in a week, it is not clutter, it is an activity with nowhere else to be, and no table standard will survive it. Give that activity a caddy it lives in and a named shelf it goes back to, or accept that this is a desk and stop calling the room a dining room. Then decide which meal you are protecting, Sunday lunch or weeknight dinner, say it out loud to the household, and let everything outside that meal be negotiable.

watch_for.question: Burn or fire
watch_for.text: Candles set at the ends of a table runner catch the runner before anyone sitting at the table notices, and a hot serving dish on bare wood scorches it and can crack a glass top.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: A drop leaf or an extension table with a worn latch can fold on a hand when someone leans on it, and dining chairs work loose at the rungs long before they actually break.

leave_behind.standard: Bare wood plus one centerpiece between meals, and every visiting activity arrives in its own container and leaves with it.
leave_behind.trigger: When the plates go to the sink after dinner, everything else on the table travels with them.

shine_detail.shine_summary: Clean the table to read it. Crumbs and spills hide in the seams and joints, so work the whole piece top to bottom and back to front, not just the open top where the plates sat.

surfaces.surface: The tabletop and the centerpiece footprint
surfaces.method: Clear the top to bare wood, then wipe the whole surface with a cloth just damp with neutral pH cleaner, working the full length in one direction. Go back over it with a dry microfiber cloth so no moisture sits on the finish, and lift the centerpiece to get the ring of dust it leaves rather than wiping around it.

surfaces.surface: The leaf seam or extension joint
surfaces.method: Run a fingernail wrapped in a thin cloth down the seam where the leaves meet, because that gap holds crumbs a flat wipe skates straight over. On an extension table, open it a hand's width and clean into the exposed slides before you close it again.

surfaces.surface: The underside lip and apron rail
surfaces.method: Wipe the underside edge and the apron rail where hands grip to pull a chair in, since that band goes untouched for months and turns tacky. Take a dry cloth first for cobwebs, then a barely damp one.

surfaces.surface: The pedestal, legs, and casters
surfaces.method: Dust from the top of the pedestal down to the feet, working into the carved detail and the caster wheels where dust and hair wrap around the axle.

surfaces.surface: The chair seats and back rails
surfaces.method: Wipe each seat and back rail with the neutral cleaner and dry a wood seat at once. Vacuum a fabric seat with the upholstery tool along the front edge where crumbs drop.

surfaces.surface: The chair rungs and stretchers
surfaces.method: Wipe every rung and the low stretcher bars, the ones that never get touched, working the cloth right into the joints where they meet the legs.

surfaces.surface: The floor under the table
surfaces.method: Push the chairs out and vacuum the whole footprint under the table with the floor tool, then run it along the skirting behind where the table usually stands.

inspect_as_you_clean: Lifting veneer or a bubbling finish along the leaf seam tells you water has crept under the surface. Flag it.
A white heat ring or a scorch bloom appearing as you wipe is the mark of a hot dish set straight on the wood. Flag where it sits.
A screw backing out of the apron, or a top fixing you can rock with a fingertip, means the frame is working loose. Flag it.
On an extension table, a leaf latch that no longer sits flush or a slide that binds is worth flagging while the leaf is open.

zones.time_note: most of it in Sort, because giving each piece of paper a verdict is the slow part
zones.purpose: Hold serving dishes during a meal and a small, deliberate display between them.
zones.done_looks_like: A taped run of bare wood at the end nearest the table long enough for the roasting pan, three display objects grouped at the lamp end, no paper on the wood, and the lamp cord the only cord in sight.

passes.sort: Take everything off the wood, including the picture frames and the candlesticks, and give every piece of paper a verdict tonight: act on it, file it, or recycle it. Burnt-down candle stubs, dried flowers, and chargers belonging to other rooms leave now.
passes.straighten: Keep the end nearest the table entirely bare for setting dishes down, and group whatever display you keep at the far end near the lamp. Serving spoons and the trivet stack live in the top drawer directly beneath that bare end.
passes.shine: Lift each object rather than dusting around it, then work the wax drips off with a plastic card and gentle warmth, and treat the pale rings left by cold glasses. Dust behind the frames and along the back edge where the wall meets the wood.
passes.safety: Trace the lamp cord from the shade to the outlet and count everything else sharing that plug, because a sideboard collects a lamp, a charger, and a warming tray on one socket hidden behind heavy furniture nobody pulls out. Move any candle sitting within arm's reach of a curtain or a wall hanging.
passes.standardize: The taped run stays bare, always, and the display group is three objects at most. If you cannot set the roasting pan down without moving something first, the standard has already slipped.
passes.sustain: Nothing sleeps on this wood overnight except the lamp and the three display pieces, so the last thing that comes off it each night is whatever arrived that day.

the_call.title: The clear run you actually need
the_call.text: You have been asking one surface to do three jobs: serving, display, and mail. It cannot, and the mail always wins, because paper arrives daily and decor does not. Settle it with a measurement rather than an intention. Take the largest dish you genuinely serve from this surface, the roasting pan or the big salad bowl, set it down where you would really set it, and mark that length of wood with a strip of tape. That run is protected and nothing lives on it, ever. Now look at your decor in what is left. Whatever does not fit in the remaining length leaves the room, however much you like it, and the mail never had a claim here to begin with.

watch_for.question: Burn or fire
watch_for.text: A sideboard often ends up carrying a lamp, a phone charger, and a warming tray on one outlet behind the furniture where you never look. Count what is on that plug and feel the strip for warmth or discoloring.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: Tall vases and heavy candlesticks on a narrow sideboard sit at head height for a small child and topple when the drawer below is yanked open.

leave_behind.standard: The taped serving run stays bare, three display objects at the far end, and no paper on the wood at any hour.
leave_behind.trigger: When the day's mail comes through the door, it goes straight past this surface to the chair where you actually open it.

shine_detail.shine_summary: The sideboard earns its keep at meals and shows off between them, so lift every object and clean the wood itself. Wax, cold-glass rings, and the dust line along the wall are the three things a quick pass leaves behind.

surfaces.surface: The display objects, vases, and candlesticks
surfaces.method: Lift each object off rather than dusting around it. Wipe it in your hands, and use the detail brush to reach into the fluting of a candlestick and the neck of a vase where dust packs down hard.

surfaces.surface: The picture frames and their glass
surfaces.method: Dust the frame tops, then wipe the glass with streak-free cleaner sprayed onto the cloth, never onto the frame, so no liquid runs behind the glass onto the photo.

surfaces.surface: The wood top, wax drips, and water rings
surfaces.method: Wipe the cleared wood with a cloth just damp with neutral pH cleaner and dry it at once. Work the wax off with the edge of a plastic card and a little gentle warmth from your hand until it lifts, then treat the pale rings a cold glass left.

surfaces.surface: The back edge and the wall seam
surfaces.method: Vacuum the crumbs from the seam where the wood meets the wall, then run the detail brush along that back edge and behind the frame stands where a wipe cannot reach.

surfaces.surface: The lamp, shade, and its cord run
surfaces.method: Dust the shade top and the bulb when cold, wipe the lamp base, then follow the cord back and wipe it as you go, handling its whole length rather than only the visible part.

surfaces.surface: The drawer fronts and pulls
surfaces.method: Wipe the drawer fronts and work the cloth around each pull and keyplate where fingers leave a smudge.

inspect_as_you_clean: As you lift the lamp and run the cord through your hand, flag any cracked, brittle, or chafed section, and an outlet face or plug that has browned.
A water ring that will not lift, with a soft or spongy patch of finish under it, means moisture is sitting there. Flag it.
Fresh pinholes with a little powder beneath, or a leg you can rock, say the frame is working loose or being eaten. Flag it.
A scorch bloom or a heat ring you had not seen before points to something hot being set down here. Flag where it is.

zones.time_note: the linens take the bulk of it, the serving pieces go quickly
zones.purpose: Hold the things that only come out when the table is being set.
zones.done_looks_like: Two tablecloths rolled with their matching napkins inside them in one drawer, serving bowls nested by size in the next, the large platters standing on edge behind a divider, taper candles of one length in a latched drawer, and a count card taped inside the door.

passes.sort: Pull every tablecloth, runner, and napkin out and lay them across the table so you can see which sets are actually complete. Partial napkin sets, cloths with stains you have already tried and failed to lift, and serving pieces orphaned from sets you no longer own are finished.
passes.straighten: Give linens one drawer and serving pieces another, and stand the big platters on edge behind a divider so you stop lifting three to reach the fourth. Roll each cloth with its matching napkins inside it so one pull brings out everything the table needs.
passes.shine: Wipe the shelves and the drawer runners while they are empty, then smell the linens, because a musty note means something went away damp and needs rewashing before it goes back. Check the silver-plate serving pieces for tarnish while you can see all of them at once.
passes.safety: Heavy stoneware platters and the punch bowl go on the lowest shelf and never above shoulder height, because they come down while your hands are already full. If taper candles and long matches live loose in a low drawer, move them to a latched drawer or a high shelf out of a child's reach.
passes.standardize: Tape a count card inside the door: two cloths, one runner, eight napkins, four serving spoons. A ninth napkin arriving as a gift means an older one becomes a rag that same evening.
passes.sustain: When a tablecloth comes out of the dryer, it goes back rolled with its napkins inside before it ever touches the back of a chair.

the_call.title: The tablecloth for a table you don't own
the_call.text: This drawer is full of linen from other houses, other tables, and other decades, and you keep it because letting go of good cloth feels wasteful. Make it a measuring problem instead of a feeling. Measure your table, then measure every cloth: one that does not hang at least a hand's depth over your actual table edge on all sides will never get used, because it looks wrong the moment it goes on and you will fold it away again. Keep the cloths that fit the table you own, plus one sized for the table with the leaf in. Anything carrying a stain you have already treated once and failed to shift becomes rags today, not next season. Partial napkin sets travel with the cloth they match, or they go with it.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: Platters and the punch bowl stored above shoulder height come down while your arms are already loaded, and a drawer packed tight with linens can pull clean out of its runners.

watch_for.question: Burn or fire
watch_for.text: Boxes of taper candles and long matches sitting loose in a low sideboard drawer are exactly at a child's reach and open on all sides.

leave_behind.standard: A written count card inside the door, linens rolled with their napkins, platters on edge, and the heavy pieces on the bottom shelf.
leave_behind.trigger: When the tablecloth comes out of the dryer, it is rolled and returned before anything else in that load gets folded.

shine_detail.shine_summary: This is where the meal-only things live, so clean it empty and use your nose as much as your cloth. A musty linen or a spreading tarnish is only catchable while everything is out at once.

surfaces.surface: The shelf boards
surfaces.method: Take each shelf empty, vacuum the corners, then wipe the boards with a barely damp neutral pH cloth and dry them before anything returns.

surfaces.surface: The drawer interiors and dividers
surfaces.method: Lift out any divider and vacuum the grit from the drawer base and its corners, then wipe the interior and dry it fully, because a damp drawer is what a rolled tablecloth soaks up.

surfaces.surface: The drawer runners
surfaces.method: Wipe both runners and the underside of the drawer, then slide it a few times to check it still runs flush before you refill it.

surfaces.surface: The linens
surfaces.method: Air each tablecloth and napkin and smell it as you fold it back in. A musty note means it went away damp and wants rewashing, not restacking.

surfaces.surface: The nested serving bowls and platters on edge
surfaces.method: Wipe the dust from the top bowl of each nest and from the platters standing on edge, getting the rims and the feet where dust settles on the upturned edge.

surfaces.surface: The silver-plate serving pieces
surfaces.method: Dust each piece and look at all of them together for tarnish while they are out. A spoon that is dulling wants silver polish worked in with a soft cloth, then buffed off, which this zone's supplies do not carry.

surfaces.surface: The door interior and count card
surfaces.method: Wipe the inside of the door and the count card taped to it so the numbers stay readable.

inspect_as_you_clean: A musty or damp smell in the linens or the drawer, or a water stain darkening the back of a low shelf, points to moisture getting in. Flag it.
Tarnish spreading across the silver-plate, especially in the crevices, is worth flagging while you can see every piece side by side.
A shelf board bowing under the stoneware, or a runner pulling away from its screws, is a fixing starting to fail. Flag it.
A hairline crack across a platter or a chip on the punch bowl rim can open into a break the next time it is carried full. Flag the piece.

zones.time_note: close to half of it is hand-washing and drying
zones.purpose: Keep the good tableware safe, visible, and genuinely usable.
zones.done_looks_like: Plates stacked no more than eight high with felt between them, cups standing single file rather than nested, glasses rim up on a clean liner, tureens on the bottom shelf, the cabinet strapped to a wall stud, and a photo of the finished shelves taped inside the door.

passes.sort: Take every piece out and split it into three groups: complete sets, chipped or crazed pieces, and lone survivors of sets that are long gone. A chipped rim cannot be mended and is not safe to drink from, so that whole group leaves together.
passes.straighten: Tureens and heavy serving pieces on the bottom shelf, plates and bowls at hand height, ceremonial pieces up top. Stack plates no more than eight high with felt or a paper plate between them, and stand cups single file instead of nesting them into each other.
passes.shine: Wash by hand in a plastic basin with a towel in the bottom, never the dishwasher for gilt rims or hand painting, and dry each piece straight away rather than leaving it to drain. Clean the cabinet glass inside and out and wipe the shelf liners while the shelves are bare.
passes.safety: Strap the cabinet to a wall stud, because a tall glass-fronted case loaded with plates is the heaviest tip-over risk in this room and its shelves are the right shape for a child to climb. Do not serve food or drink from decorative antique or hand-painted pieces of unknown origin, since older glazes can carry lead.
passes.standardize: Photograph the finished shelves and tape the picture inside the door so the china goes back the same way after every holiday. When a shelf no longer matches its photo, something is missing or broken and you find out that day rather than next Christmas.
passes.sustain: After any meal that used the good china, it is hand-washed, dried, and back behind the glass before anyone turns the kitchen light off.

the_call.title: The twelve settings from your grandmother
the_call.text: This is the hardest decision in the room and everyone knows why: the china is not china, it is a person. Separate the two on purpose. Keep the number of settings that fits the largest meal you have actually hosted in the past three years, plus two for breakage. For the rest, write down whose they were and what you remember about them, photograph them alongside that note, and offer them to the relative most likely to set a table with them, then sell or donate whatever nobody claims. Then the part people skip: what you keep, you owe use. Name an occasion, once a year at minimum, when it goes on the table. China that never leaves the cabinet is not being honored. It is being stored behind glass.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: A tall glass-fronted cabinet loaded with heavy plates is the largest tip-over risk in this room, and its shelves make an inviting ladder for a small child.

watch_for.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
watch_for.text: Decorative antique and hand-painted pieces of unknown origin can carry lead in the glaze, particularly on gilt rims and bright reds. Display them, but keep acidic food and drink off them.

leave_behind.standard: A shelf photo inside the door, eight plates at most per stack with felt between, the weight on the bottom shelf, and the cabinet strapped to the wall.
leave_behind.trigger: When the last guest leaves, the good china is washed and back behind the glass before anyone turns the kitchen light off.

shine_detail.shine_summary: The good china only stays usable if the cabinet holding it is sound. Wash by hand, clean the glass inside and out, and read the cabinet itself while the shelves are bare.

surfaces.surface: The top of the cabinet
surfaces.method: Dust the very top of the case, high and out of sight, where this room's dust settles thickest and nobody ever looks. Take a dry cloth first, then a barely damp one, and dry the wood after.

surfaces.surface: The glass doors and front, inside and out
surfaces.method: Spray streak-free cleaner onto the cloth, not the glass, and clean both faces of each pane. Run the detail brush along the glazing bars and into the corners of the frame where the cloth misses.

surfaces.surface: The interior glass shelves and liners
surfaces.method: With the shelves bare, wipe the glass shelves and the liners, getting the shelf edges and the support pins where dust and grit collect.

surfaces.surface: The china itself
surfaces.method: Wash each piece by hand in a plastic basin with a towel in the bottom, never the dishwasher for a gilt rim or hand painting. Dry each piece straight away rather than leaving it to drain, and set it back rim up on a clean liner.

surfaces.surface: The cabinet frame and hardware
surfaces.method: Wipe the wooden frame, the hinges, the lock, and the strap point where the case meets the wall, using the detail brush on the hinge knuckles.

surfaces.surface: The lower shelf and tureens
surfaces.method: Wipe the bottom shelf and the tureens standing on it, getting under the foot of each where a ring of dust collects.

inspect_as_you_clean: As you clear the shelves, flag a glass shelf with a hairline crack or a chipped edge, or a support pin that is bent or missing, since any of those can let a loaded shelf drop.
A door that no longer closes flush, or a sagging hinge, is the frame moving. Flag it.
A wall strap that looks frayed or a fixing screw you can see has pulled loose is worth flagging, even though bracing it is the Safety pass.
Moisture or condensation inside the glass, or a back panel starting to bow, tells you damp is getting in. Flag it.

zones.time_note: the descaling cycle runs while you sort the tea boxes
zones.purpose: Make a drink and hand it over without crossing into the kitchen.
zones.done_looks_like: Machine, grounds, mugs, then spoons and sugar running left to right along one liftable tray, mugs capped at the number of daily drinkers plus two, a marked fill line on the bean jar, and a hand's width of clear air behind the kettle.

passes.sort: Line up every tea box, syrup bottle, and pod sleeve and check the dates, then open the travel mugs and match them to their lids. Anything past date, any mug missing its lid, and the promotional glassware you have never once poured into are out.
passes.straighten: Set the station in the order your hands actually move: machine, then grounds or pods, then mugs, then spoons and sugar, then the way out toward the table. Leave a hand's width behind the kettle so its steam is not hitting the underside of a shelf.
passes.shine: Descale the machine on the interval its manual gives, lift the drip tray grate and wash underneath it where mould starts, and get the sticky ring from under the syrup bottle. Rinse the kettle and look at the element for scale while you are there.
passes.safety: Water and electricity share this counter, so give the machine and kettle their own outlet, keep cords back from the edge where a sleeve can hook them, and never refill a plugged-in machine over its own base. If wine or spirits live here, they belong behind a latch or high up, not on an open shelf at a child's eye level.
passes.standardize: Mugs are capped at daily drinkers plus two, and the bean or pod jar carries a marked fill line that tells you when to buy more. Everything sits on one tray you can lift with one hand, so the counter underneath cleans in a single wipe.
passes.sustain: While the morning coffee is brewing, you wipe the tray and top the jar back up to its line.

the_call.title: The second machine
the_call.text: There are at least two ways to make a hot drink on this counter, and one of them is kept for the person you meant to become. Do not settle it from memory, because memory is generous about the press you used enthusiastically for three weeks the summer you bought it. Put a sticky note on each machine and make a mark every time it produces a drink someone actually drinks. Give it one full week, weekend included. Any machine with fewer than three marks comes off the counter and goes into a cupboard for one more month, and if it is still unused at the end of that month it leaves the house. The same test settles the mug shelf: the mugs you reach past every single morning are not favorites, they are furniture.

watch_for.question: Water and electricity
watch_for.text: The machine, the kettle, and an open water jug share a small surface, and cords near the front edge get hooked by a sleeve. Keep the appliances on their own outlet and never top up a plugged-in machine over its base.

watch_for.question: Burn or fire
watch_for.text: A kettle boiling directly under a wall shelf drives steam into the underside of it, warping the shelf and dropping condensation onto the plug below.

watch_for.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
watch_for.text: Wine and spirits on an open dining-room shelf sit unlatched at child height, which is rarely true of anything in the kitchen.

leave_behind.standard: One tray, one outlet, use-order left to right, mugs capped at drinkers plus two, and a fill line on the jar.
leave_behind.trigger: While the morning coffee brews, the tray gets wiped and the jar gets topped back to its line.

shine_detail.shine_summary: A drinks station runs on water and heat, so descale it, clear the sticky rings, and clean the hidden underside of the drip tray where mold starts. Cleaning it close is also how you catch a tired cord or a warping shelf.

surfaces.surface: The wall shelf and its underside
surfaces.method: Wipe the top of the wall shelf and, more importantly, its underside above the kettle, where steam warps the board and drops condensation. Get the cloth right up to the wall.

surfaces.surface: The counter and the liftable tray
surfaces.method: Lift the whole tray, wipe the counter beneath it, then wipe the tray itself, working food-area degreaser into the coffee splatter and drying after.

surfaces.surface: The machine, drip tray, and grate
surfaces.method: Wipe the machine body with a barely damp cloth, keeping water off the buttons and the plug, then lift the drip tray grate out and wash under it in the sink, because that hidden well is where mold starts. Descale the machine on the interval its manual gives, since the supplies here do not cover that.

surfaces.surface: The kettle body and element
surfaces.method: Unplug it, wipe the kettle body, rinse the inside, and look at the element for scale. Heavy scale wants a descaler, not a cloth.

surfaces.surface: The bean jar, grinder, and syrup bottles
surfaces.method: Wipe the bean jar and its fill line, brush grounds out of the grinder throat with the machine off and unplugged, and lift the syrup bottle to clean the sticky ring welded to the shelf under it.

surfaces.surface: The mugs and their shelf
surfaces.method: Wipe the mug shelf and the base of each mug where a coffee ring dries onto the shelf.

surfaces.surface: The cords and the air gap behind the kettle
surfaces.method: Wipe each cord along its length and clear the hand's width of air behind the kettle so nothing sits against a hot wall.

inspect_as_you_clean: As you run each cord through your hand, flag a cracked, frayed, or stiff section, and a plug or outlet face that has browned.
Soft black mold in the seam of the drip tray or under the grate is worth flagging, not just wiping past.
A shelf underside that is swelling, warping, or discoloring above the kettle is steam damage building. Flag it.
Water pooling under the machine base when it should be dry can mean an inside seal is going. Flag it.

rooms.intro: The living room belongs to everybody, which is why nobody puts anything away in it. Six people can pass through in an evening and each leave one object behind, and by Sunday the sofa has a laundry pile and the coffee table has four mugs. Start with the floor and the coffee table, because those two are what you see from the doorway, and a room that looks reset from the doorway is a room people keep resetting.

tips.label: Where to start
tips.text: Do the Floor and Circulation Path first, with a laundry basket in your hand. Everything on the floor rides the basket out, and you get an honest look at how much of this room's mess is shoes, school bags and toys from other rooms just visiting.

tips.label: Cleaning note
tips.text: Lift every seat cushion before you vacuum, not after. The seams hold crumbs, coins, hair clips and the remote you replaced last month, and the upholstery tool only reaches what you have already exposed.

tips.label: The trap
tips.text: This room fails by donation, not by neglect. Each person drops one thing and considers the room fine, so no single household member ever sees a mess they caused. Standards here have to be visible from the sofa, which means a throw basket with a label on it and a coffee table tray you can see is overflowing from across the room.

zones.time_note: most of it in Sort, because the cushion seams and the throw pile take longer than you expect
zones.purpose: Somewhere every person in the house can sit down without first moving something.
zones.done_looks_like: Every seat on the sofa and every armchair is sittable without lifting a single thing off it. Throws folded to one size in one basket, at most one cushion per seat left in place, and both remotes in the tray on the arm with batteries that work.

passes.sort: Pull everything off the seats and dig the seams out: the laundry that migrated here, the second and third throw blanket, the magazines wedged behind the armrest, the coins and hair ties down the back. Sort into leaves-the-room, goes-in-the-wash, and lives-here.
passes.straighten: The remotes get one tray, and it goes on the arm people actually reach from while sitting, not the arm nearest the television. Throws get one basket at the end of the sofa, and reading matter gets one slot, so nothing has to be lifted off a cushion before someone sits.
passes.shine: Vacuum the seams and the deck under the cushions with the upholstery tool, then wipe the arms and the headrest where hands and hair oil land. Rotate and flip the cushions so the seat nobody chooses takes a turn at the wear.
passes.safety: Check the recliner footrest and the sofa bed hinge, and make it a rule that both close slowly with a look at the floor first, because that is where a child sits. Throws that trail off the sofa onto the floor are what people step on when they stand up in the dark, so the basket keeps them off the walkway.
passes.standardize: Put the rule on the basket label itself: throws folded into the basket, nothing stored on a seat. "A standard is the best way you know today, written down."
passes.sustain: The last person out of the room at night squares the cushions and drops the throws in the basket. It takes the length of turning the lamp off.

the_call.title: The pillows you move to sit down
the_call.text: Count the decorative pillows you shift onto the floor every single time you sit. Those are not seating, and they are not decor either, because decor stays where it is put. Keep only the number that can stay in place while a person sits, which is usually one per armchair and often zero on the sofa people flop on. The honest reason you have been avoiding this is that somebody bought them for you. Keep one of that set and let the other three go without a ceremony.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: Recliner footrests and sofa bed frames close hard on fingers and small feet, especially with a child sitting on the floor in front of the chair.

watch_for.question: Fall
watch_for.text: A throw blanket hanging off the sofa onto the floor is the classic night-time trip, because you stand up from that exact spot in the dark.

leave_behind.standard: Seats hold people, not storage. Throws live folded in one basket, remotes in one tray.
leave_behind.trigger: When you switch the lamp off for the night, the cushions get squared and the throws go in the basket.

shine_detail.shine_summary: Most of what a sofa swallows lives in the seams and the deck under the cushions, so work from the headrest down and lift every cushion out. Start high where hair oil lands, finish under the front edge where the crumbs and coins settle.

surfaces.surface: The backrest and headrest tops
surfaces.method: Start at the top with the vacuum's upholstery tool along the headrest and backrest, then wipe the headrest band with a barely damp microfiber cloth, since this is where hair oil and hand grease settle. On leather or vinyl, follow with a dry cloth so no moisture sits in the grain.

surfaces.surface: The arms and the front roll
surfaces.method: Vacuum the tops and sides of the arms, then wipe them with a cloth wrung out in neutral pH cleaner and buff dry. The arms take the most hand contact, so give them the same second pass you gave the headrest.

surfaces.surface: The seat cushions, both faces
surfaces.method: Lift each seat cushion out, vacuum both faces and the piping with the upholstery tool, then flip and rotate them so the seat nobody chooses takes a turn at the wear before it goes back.

surfaces.surface: The deck and the seams under the cushions
surfaces.method: With the cushions out, run the crevice tool right into the seam where the deck meets the back and along the front rail, working back to front. This hidden well is where crumbs, coins and pet hair collect and stay.

surfaces.surface: The throw pillows and the folded throws
surfaces.method: Take the throw pillows outside and beat them, vacuum the covers, and launder the throws, even the ones that look clean, because this is where pet hair concentrates. Fold them back to one size in the basket rather than over the sofa back.

surfaces.surface: The remote tray on the arm
surfaces.method: Empty the tray, wipe it and the remotes with a cloth just damp with neutral pH cleaner, and dry them. Sticky buttons are usually grime rather than a dead battery.

surfaces.surface: The outer back and the sides of the frame
surfaces.method: Pull the sofa forward and vacuum the outer back and the two sides with the upholstery tool, then wipe them with a barely damp cloth and dry any leather or vinyl. On a sofa that lives against a wall this panel goes months untouched and holds a grey film of dust.

surfaces.surface: The base, feet and skirt
surfaces.method: Finish at the floor line: vacuum along the skirt and reach the crevice tool under the front edge, where dust drifts into the shadow beneath the frame.

products_used: Compact vacuum with attachments (upholstery and crevice tools)
Upholstery spot cleaner for a set-in stain (not in this zone's list)
inspect_as_you_clean: A musty smell or a damp patch deep in the seat foam, where a drink went down between the cushions and never dried out
Frame timber that flexes, or a joint that creaks when you press down on the arm
Split seam stitching, a broken zip pull, or foam crumbling at a cushion corner
Coins, a battery, or a pen cap surfacing from the crevice, small things that have slipped down out of reach
Fabric worn shiny or thin on the seat everyone chooses

zones.time_note: quick, with most of it spent deciding what leaves rather than cleaning
zones.purpose: A small shared surface for whatever is happening right now, and nothing that is not.
zones.done_looks_like: One tray holding four coasters and the remote in use, plus at most one book or one plant beside it. No mugs, no charging cables, no post, and the wood or glass showing across most of the top.

passes.sort: Clear the whole top onto the floor and put back only what somebody used in the last two days. The candle burned down to the foil, the coasters nobody uses because they sit on the far corner, the three-month-old magazines and the takeaway menus all go now.
passes.straighten: The tray sets the table's entire standing inventory. Coasters go on it within arm's reach of whoever sits on the sofa, so a mug lands on a coaster without anyone leaning across the table.
passes.shine: Lift the tray and wipe the whole top including the ring marks, then get the underside edge and the lower shelf where crumbs and dust collect unseen. A glass top needs two passes, one for grease and one dry, or every fingerprint shows by lamplight.
passes.safety: A glass top or a hard square corner sits at exactly the height of a toddler's forehead, so corner guards or a different table is the real fix, not vigilance. A candle here is surrounded by throws, magazines and paper, which is the wrong neighbourhood for an open flame.
passes.standardize: Photograph the finished tray and keep that picture as the reference for what clear means on this table. See Chapter 25, the ideal-state photo.
passes.sustain: Whoever carries the last mug to the kitchen takes everything else that does not belong on the table with them, in the same trip.

the_call.title: The book you are in the middle of
the_call.text: There are four books on this table and you are reading one. The other three are there because putting them away feels like admitting you stopped. Here is the rule that settles it: check the bookmark. If it has not moved in two weeks, you are not reading that book, you are storing it, and storage happens on the shelf. One book per person stays on the table. This is not a judgement on the book, and you can carry it back down the moment you actually open it again.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: Glass tops and hard square corners sit at head height for a child who is learning to walk, and the edge of a coffee table is where those falls land.

watch_for.question: Burn or fire
watch_for.text: A candle on this table is surrounded by throws, magazines and paper, and it is the surface most often left burning when everyone goes to bed.

leave_behind.standard: If it does not fit on the tray, it does not live on the table.
leave_behind.trigger: When the last mug goes to the kitchen at the end of the evening, everything off-tray travels with it.

shine_detail.shine_summary: This is the shared surface that shows every ring and fingerprint, so clear it to bare wood or glass and clean the top, the underside lip, and the lower shelf. A glass top always takes two passes, one for grease and one dry.

surfaces.surface: The tabletop and its ring marks
surfaces.method: Clear everything off, then clean the whole top including the ring marks. On wood, wipe with a cloth wrung out in neutral pH cleaner and buff dry. On glass, make two passes, one with glass cleaner to lift the grease and one dry, or every fingerprint shows by lamplight.

surfaces.surface: The underside lip and apron
surfaces.method: Run a cloth around the underside edge where hands grip to pull the table closer. This rim holds a greasy film you feel but never see.

surfaces.surface: The lower shelf or magazine tier
surfaces.method: Take everything off the lower shelf and wipe it, corners included, since crumbs and dust settle here unseen while the top looks clean.

surfaces.surface: The legs and feet
surfaces.method: Wipe down the legs, look at the feet pads as you reach them, then vacuum the floor shadow the table casts before you set it back in place.

surfaces.surface: The tray and coasters
surfaces.method: Wipe the tray and both faces of every coaster. A coaster that sticks to a glass is holding old spill.

products_used: Streak-free glass cleaner for a glass top (not in this zone's list)
inspect_as_you_clean: A hairline crack or a chipped edge in a glass top catching the cloth as it passes
A leg that rocks or a joint that gives when you lean on a corner
A pale heat bloom or a soft, lifting patch in a wood finish where a hot mug sat too long
The lower shelf board bowing in the middle under stacked books

zones.time_note: most of it behind the unit, sorting cables and working out what is still plugged into what
zones.purpose: Keep the television, sound and consoles working, cool and cabled so a fault is findable.
zones.done_looks_like: Every cable labelled at both ends, running in one bundle to a single labelled power strip. Nothing plugged in that serves a device you no longer own, a clear hand's gap of air around the amplifier and console vents, and every game controller and remote in one bin instead of four locations.

passes.sort: Unplug and lay out every cable, then name the device each one serves. The composite leads, the disc player nobody has loaded in a year, the streaming stick from two televisions ago and the charger with the old connector all leave. Discs and games get one decision each: sell, lend, or recycle.
passes.straighten: Bundle the cables by device path with velcro ties so one console can be pulled out without disturbing the sound bar. Controllers and remotes get one ventilated bin, set at the height of whoever plays, not on top of the unit where they slide behind it.
passes.shine: Vacuum the dust off the console and amplifier vents and the whole back panel of the television, because dust is what turns a warm device into a hot one. Wipe the screen with a dry microfiber cloth only, never a spray.
passes.safety: Heat and power are the two hazards behind this unit: keep the vents unblocked, never run one power strip into another, and look at every cable for a cracked or scorched section as you handle it. Anchor the television to the wall or to the unit, because a screen tipping off the front edge is the single worst thing this room can do to a child.
passes.standardize: Label both ends of a cable the day it goes in and label the strip's outlets to match, so a cable that belongs to nothing is obvious at a glance. See Chapter 14, visual controls.
passes.sustain: When you swap a device in or add one, it does not get switched on until its cable is labelled at both ends.

the_call.title: The dead electronics shelf
the_call.text: Somewhere in this unit is a working device nobody has switched on in a year, and a box of cables kept because they might fit something. You have avoided this because the devices cost real money and letting them go feels like admitting the money is gone. The money is already gone. The rule: power each device on now. If it does not boot, or it boots and nobody in the house asks for it within the month, it goes to recycling or resale this week. For a cable, name the device it serves out loud before you finish picking it up, or it leaves, because an unnamed cable will still be unnamed next year.

watch_for.question: Burn or fire
watch_for.text: Blocked console and amplifier vents, dust packed on the back of the television, and one power strip plugged into another are the fire risks here, and all three are hidden behind the unit.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: An unanchored television on a low unit tips forward when a child pulls on the edge or climbs the shelf below it.

watch_for.question: Water and electricity
watch_for.text: Drinks set on top of the console or on the floor beside the power strip put liquid directly over live connections.

leave_behind.standard: Every cable is labelled at both ends and every device has clear air on its vents.
leave_behind.trigger: When the credits roll and you switch the television off, the controllers go back in their bin on the way out of the room.

shine_detail.shine_summary: Dust is what turns a warm device into a hot one, so the real work here is the vents and the back panel, not the screen. Work top down, brush the dust out of every slot, and touch the screen with a dry cloth only.

surfaces.surface: The top of the unit
surfaces.method: Start on the top surface with a cloth just damp with neutral pH cleaner. This is the ledge where dust settles thickest.

surfaces.surface: The television screen
surfaces.method: Wipe the screen with a dry microfiber cloth only, in slow straight passes. Never spray anything onto a screen and never reach for a paper towel, which scratches the coating.

surfaces.surface: The television back panel and bezel
surfaces.method: Vacuum the whole back panel and the bezel with a brush head, working the dust out of the ridges. This is the dust that turns a warm set into a hot one.

surfaces.surface: The console and amplifier vent slots
surfaces.method: Brush and vacuum every vent slot on the top and back of each device. If dust has matted solid in a slot, loosen it with a soft detail brush first, then lift it away with the vacuum.

surfaces.surface: The shelf surfaces and front edges
surfaces.method: Wipe each shelf and its front edge with the damp cloth, moving devices forward rather than wiping around them.

surfaces.surface: The cable bundle, power strip and floor behind
surfaces.method: Wipe the cable bundle and the outside of the power strip with a barely damp cloth, keeping moisture away from the socket faces, and dry it. Then vacuum the floor behind the unit where dust and pet hair pack in against the wall.

surfaces.surface: The controllers and remotes
surfaces.method: Wipe the grips, buttons and thumbstick collars with a barely damp cloth and dry them. This is the grime you hand from person to person.

products_used: Small detail brush for the vent slots (not in this zone's list)
inspect_as_you_clean: A hot-plastic or scorched smell around the back panel, strongest near the amplifier
A power strip, plug, or socket face that is warm to the touch or browning at the edges
A console or amplifier fan that has grown noticeably louder than it used to run
Dust matted into a solid felt across a vent slot rather than loose enough to lift
A cable sheath gone stiff or tacky with heat where it bends behind the unit

zones.time_note: nearly all of it in Sort, because every book is its own small decision
zones.purpose: Hold the books you will genuinely open again, and a small number of objects you actually want to look at.
zones.done_looks_like: Each shelf has a hand's width of empty space at one end, books standing upright between bookends with nothing stacked flat on top of them, frames and objects gathered in two or three groups instead of spaced evenly along every shelf, and a strap running from the top of the unit into the wall.

passes.sort: Take one shelf down at a time so every book passes through your hands. Duplicates, the manuals for appliances you replaced, the free paperbacks from a conference and anything water-damaged go now. Empty frames, the dead plant and the souvenirs you stopped seeing years ago go with them.
passes.straighten: Group by how you actually hunt for a book, which for most people is subject first and author second, never colour. The heavy art and reference volumes go on the bottom shelves where a fall does no harm, and the hand's width of slack at the end of each shelf is where the next book lands.
passes.shine: Dust the top edges of the books themselves, not just the shelf boards, and wipe the shelf fronts where hands grab to pull a spine out. Do the very top of the tallest unit, which is where this room's dust actually settles and where nobody ever looks.
passes.safety: Strap the unit into the wall studs, because a tall bookcase loaded high will come over when a child uses the shelves as a ladder, and it lands loaded. Keep the stone and glass objects on the lowest shelves, and use a step, never the arm of the sofa, to reach the top.
passes.standardize: Bookends plus a small labelled marker at the front of each group makes a misfiled book visible from the doorway, without pulling a single spine out.
passes.sustain: When you finish a book, it goes back into its group that same evening instead of onto the coffee table.

the_call.title: Books you keep to be the person who read them
the_call.text: A shelf is partly an argument about who you are, and that is why sorting one is uncomfortable. Separate the two questions. First: would you open this again, or press it into a friend's hand and say read this? If yes, it stays, no further debate. If no, ask the second question honestly: are you keeping it so a visitor sees it? That is a fine reason for two or three books and a bad reason for forty. Unread books get a single shelf, capped between two bookends. When a new one arrives and it does not fit, one leaves. Nobody is grading you on the books you did not get to.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: A tall bookcase that is not strapped to the wall tips forward when a child climbs the lower shelves, and it lands loaded.

watch_for.question: Fall
watch_for.text: Reaching the top shelf from the sofa arm or a dining chair is how people fall in this room, and it happens with an armful of books already in one hand.

leave_behind.standard: Every shelf keeps a hand's width of empty space, and the unit stays strapped to the wall.
leave_behind.trigger: When you finish a book, it goes back to its group before you start the next one.

shine_detail.shine_summary: The dust in this zone sits where nobody looks, on the very top of the unit and along the top edges of the books themselves. Work down shelf by shelf, pulling each row of books forward to reach the band behind them.

surfaces.surface: The very top of the tallest unit
surfaces.method: Start on the top of the tallest unit with a slightly damp cloth. This out-of-sight ledge is where the room's dust actually lands and where nobody ever looks.

surfaces.surface: The top edges of the books
surfaces.method: Draw a dry cloth or a soft brush along the top edges of the books, front to back, not just the shelf board. Tip a few forward and dust the head of the pages while you are there.

surfaces.surface: The shelf fronts and edges
surfaces.method: Wipe the shelf front edges where fingers grab to pull a spine out. That grip line is the greasiest part of the whole unit.

surfaces.surface: The shelf boards behind the books
surfaces.method: Slide each row of books forward and wipe the board and the dust band along the back, then stand the books back upright between the bookends.

surfaces.surface: The frames and display objects
surfaces.method: Lift each frame and object and dust under and behind it rather than around it, using a soft brush for anything carved or grooved.

surfaces.surface: The base and skirting of the unit
surfaces.method: Finish at the bottom: vacuum the base and the skirting behind the unit, and look over the wall strap while you are down there.

products_used: Soft dusting brush for carved objects (not in this zone's list)
inspect_as_you_clean: A shelf board bowed in the middle under the weight of the books standing on it
A shelf pin or bracket that has crept out of its hole so one side sits lower than the other
The wall strap gone slack, or a fixing screw that has backed out of its anchor
Damp-swollen boards, foxing on the pages, or a musty note on books stood against an outside wall

zones.time_note: short, with most of it in Safety sorting out the lamp cord and whatever is loose in the little dish
zones.purpose: Put a light, a drink and one or two personal things within reach of the chair without turning the table into a nightstand.
zones.done_looks_like: One small tray per table with no more than four items on it, a coaster under the glass, a bulb that lights and has been wiped, and the lamp cord clipped down the table leg so no cable crosses the floor to the chair.

passes.sort: Empty the little dish and the drawer onto the seat of the chair. The reading glasses with the wrong prescription, the dried-out pens, the foreign coins, the loose tablets, the charger for a phone nobody in the house owns and the coasters that never made it back to the coffee table each get a verdict now.
passes.straighten: One tray per table sets the limit, and it sits on the side the person in that chair reaches from without leaning. The phone charger gets a single clip at the table edge so the cable stays up on the table instead of hanging into the walkway.
passes.shine: Wipe the bulb and the inside of the shade while the lamp is off and cool, then the table top and the ring marks hiding under the tray. A dusty bulb throws noticeably less light, and light is the whole reason this table has a lamp on it.
passes.safety: Water and electricity meet here more than anywhere else in the room, so the glass goes on the opposite side of the tray from the lamp base and the charger. Loose tablets in an open dish sit at chair height, which is grab height for a toddler, and the lamp cord must never cross the path between the chair and the door.
