surfaces.method: Let the bulbs cool, dust the fitting and shade with a dry cloth, and lift the cobwebs off the top of each arm with the vacuum's soft brush attachment. Keep every cloth dry near the fitting.

surfaces.surface: The wall along the turn
surfaces.method: Wipe the wall itself with a barely damp cloth and a little neutral pH cleaner, giving the grey line at shoulder height an extra pass, since that is where bags, shoulders, and laundry baskets rub as people round the turn.

surfaces.surface: Behind each frame, the wire and hook
surfaces.method: As you take your hand off each frame, tilt it slightly and lift the dust off the wire and the hook behind it.

surfaces.surface: The skirting at the foot of the wall and the landing floor
surfaces.method: Finish low: vacuum the crevice along the skirting, wipe the board, then damp mop the landing floor beneath with a cleaner matched to its material.

inspect_as_you_clean: As your hand leaves each frame, look at the wire for kinks or rust and at the hook for a bent or opening lip, and flag any frame you find hanging from a single nail or a sawtooth hanger.
Push gently up under the mirror as you wipe it and note any play or movement against the wall.
Watch the wall along the turn for a soft, bulging, or stained patch that can mean damp tracking down behind the plaster.
On a sconce, notice a warm or discoloured fitting, a scorched shade, or a bulb that flickers as you dust near it.
Flag any frame that has crept out of line or drooped since last time, since the constant vibration of a stair wall is what quietly works hardware loose.

zones.time_note: most of it in Safety, walking the flight tread by tread and fixing what you find
zones.purpose: The treads, runner, handrail and lighting that carry every person in the house between floors, several times a day, often with their arms full.
zones.done_looks_like: Every tread bare from nose to riser, including the bottom three steps that usually stage things. The runner lies flat with no lifted corner at the turn. The handrail runs unbroken and unobstructed from the top newel post to the bottom, with no bag, coat or dog lead hung on either post. Both switches work, so the top step and the bottom step are lit before you take them.

passes.sort: Nothing lives on stairs. Clear the folded laundry, the shoes, the box that has sat on step four since the weekend, all of it in one trip, and put each thing where it belongs on its own floor rather than restaging it on the landing above.
passes.straighten: The one thing that must stay reachable here is the handrail, so strip both newel posts of coats, bags and leads. If a stair gate is fitted, set the top gate to swing away from the flight and never out over it.
passes.shine: Vacuum the tread noses, the crevice where each tread meets its riser, and along the stringer where a runner is tucked. That trapped grit is what polishes a runner slick under a stocking foot. Wipe the handrail its full length, including the underside your fingers wrap around.
passes.safety: Walk the flight slowly and test as you go: press each tread nose for movement, tug each runner edge, and grip the rail hard at top, middle and bottom to find a loose bracket. Then stand at the bottom in the dark and look at the top step, and stand at the top and look at the bottom. A burnt-out bulb over a top step is the single most dangerous thing in this room. Find it, and fix it now.
passes.standardize: The standard is one sentence anyone in the house can check: bare treads, full width, lit at both ends, rail clear. Photograph the empty flight from the bottom and put that picture where the staging happens, which is almost always beside the bottom step.
passes.sustain: The last person up at night takes the flight with one hand on the rail and carries whatever is sitting on a tread. If their hands are too full to hold the rail, that is the signal to make two trips.

the_call.title: The runner that has already lifted once
the_call.text: If your stairs have a runner and one corner has lifted or one rod has worked loose, you have almost certainly pressed it back down and carried on. That is the decision you keep deferring, and it is the wrong shape, because a runner that has lifted once has already told you what it will do again. Choose today between two honest options and refuse the third. Either refix it properly along its whole length, with rods or full-width tape on every tread rather than a patch on the one failed corner, or take it up entirely and live with bare treads. Bare wood you know is slippery beats a runner you have quietly stopped trusting, because you adjust your step for the first and not the second. The one thing you may not do is press it down again and wait.

watch_for.question: Fall
watch_for.text: A lifted runner corner, a loose handrail bracket, or a dead bulb over the top step. Each one is a fall on the hardest surface in the house, and they tend to arrive together, at night.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: Carrying a laundry basket or a box you cannot see over means going down blind with no free hand for the rail. Anything parked on the bottom three steps is invisible to that person.

watch_for.question: Water and electricity
watch_for.text: Changing the bulb over the stairwell means standing high on a flight with a fitting overhead. Switch the light off at the wall, let a hot bulb cool, and use a properly footed ladder from the landing rather than balancing on a tread.

watch_for.question: Fall
watch_for.text: A lifted runner corner, a loose handrail bracket, or a dead bulb over the top step. Each one is a fall on the hardest surface in the house, and they tend to arrive together, at night.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: Carrying a laundry basket or a box you cannot see over means going down blind with no free hand for the rail. Anything parked on the bottom three steps is invisible to that person.

watch_for.question: Water and electricity
watch_for.text: Changing the bulb over the stairwell means standing high on a flight with a live fitting overhead. Switch the light off at the wall, let a hot bulb cool, and work from the landing on a properly footed ladder rather than balancing on a tread.

leave_behind.standard: Bare treads at full width, runner flat and fixed the whole way, handrail clear from newel to newel, and working light at both ends.
leave_behind.trigger: When you head up to bed, you go with a hand on the rail and nothing left standing on a tread behind you.

shine_detail.shine_summary: Top to bottom and rail first: handrail, posts and balusters, then the treads, the risers, the runner and its tucked edges, and the landing floor last. The step almost everyone skips is the crevice where each tread meets its riser, and that grit is what turns a runner slick.

surfaces.surface: The handrail, full length including the underside
surfaces.method: Start with the rail. Wipe it the whole length from the top newel to the bottom, and do not skip the underside your fingers wrap around, which carries the oil off every hand that has ever used it.

surfaces.surface: Both newel posts
surfaces.method: Wipe the top and bottom newel posts, including the flat cap on top where dust settles and set-down keys leave a film.

surfaces.surface: The balusters or spindles
surfaces.method: Run a cloth or the vacuum's brush down each baluster, catching the dust that clings to the inside faces you never see head on.

surfaces.surface: The tread noses, the tread-to-riser crevice, and the riser faces
surfaces.method: Vacuum along every tread nose and right into the crevice where each tread meets its riser, since that trapped grit is exactly what polishes a runner slick under a stocking foot. Then wipe the riser faces below with a barely damp cloth, where toe scuffs and shoe marks collect the way nothing on the flat does.

surfaces.surface: The runner and its edges tucked at the stringer
surfaces.method: Vacuum the runner down the middle, then along both edges where it tucks against the stringer. Spot clean any mark with a cloth only barely damp, so the backing never soaks through.

surfaces.surface: The bare tread either side of the runner
surfaces.method: Wipe the bare wood or painted strip on each side of the runner with a cleaner matched to the material, drying as you go so no tread is left damp underfoot.

surfaces.surface: The bottom three steps
surfaces.method: Clear and clean the bottom three steps that usually end up staging things headed upstairs, so they read as stairs and not as shelves.

surfaces.surface: The landing floor, the switches, and the light fittings
surfaces.method: Finish on the flat. Vacuum and mop the landing floor, and wipe both light switches and the plate around them where every hand pushes, keeping the cloth just damp and off the switch itself.

inspect_as_you_clean: As you vacuum each tread nose, notice any tread that gives or flexes underfoot, and flag it.
Note any runner corner that has lifted as you clean the edges, and any worn strip on a nose where the pile has gone thin.
While you wipe the rail's length, notice any bracket that has worked loose or any section that turns slightly in its fixing under the cloth.
While you clean the treads under each fitting, flag a bulb over the top or bottom step that is dim, flickering, or dead, because that is the most dangerous fault this room can hold.
Watch the stringer and skirting for a cracked or springy board, and the switch plates for warmth or discolouring as you wipe them.

rooms.intro: A patio lives outdoors, which puts everything on it under a clock the indoor rooms never feel: sun makes plastic brittle, damp gets into fabric and end grain, and a season of putting things off arrives as a replacement cost. Start with the surface you walk on and the rail you lean on, because those are the only things out here that can put someone in hospital. Everything after that, the cushions and the grill and the pots, is about making the space usable within one trip through the back door.

tips.label: Where to start
tips.text: Do the Surface, Rail, and Safety Zone first, on a dry morning, before you touch a single cushion. If the boards and the railing are not sound, everything you arrange on top of them is decoration.

tips.label: Cleaning note
tips.text: Out here, cleaning is how you inspect. You will never spot a popped fastener, a soft board end, or a spider web in a burner tube while sitting in a chair. You spot them with a brush in your hand and your face close to the thing.

tips.label: The trap
tips.text: The trap is storing things outdoors that cannot live outdoors. A cushion left out overnight in dew, a cardboard box inside the deck box, a bag of charcoal resting on the ground: each is fine for a week and ruined by autumn. If it cannot take a night of rain, it belongs behind a door.

zones.time_note: most of it in Sort, deciding about cushions rather than moving chairs
zones.purpose: Seats people can drop into without checking them first, with the cushions kept dry.
zones.done_looks_like: Four chairs you can sit in without testing, set close enough to talk across, every cushion in the deck box, and no cover crumpled on the ground behind a planter.

passes.sort: Sit in every chair. The one that wobbles, the one with the cracked resin arm, and the cushion you would not offer a guest are decisions, not furniture. Count who actually sits out here on an ordinary evening and keep that many chairs plus two.
passes.straighten: Chairs face each other close enough to talk without raising your voice, and no chair sits in the swing of the back door. Cushions live in the deck box, not stacked on a seat under a towel that stays wet underneath.
passes.shine: Hose the frames and scrub the webbing where grit packs into the joints, then stand each chair on its side so water runs out of the tubing instead of sitting inside it all summer. Check the underside of every cushion for black speckling while it dries.
passes.safety: Resin and plastic chairs go brittle from years of sun long before they look it. Flex each arm and press the seat pan hard with your palm; a chair that creaks or shows fine white cracks around a leg joint leaves today, not after someone drops through it onto the boards.
passes.standardize: One cushion per seat and none spare, so a gap in the box tells you a cushion is still out on a chair. A photo of the chairs in their usual evening arrangement, taped inside the deck box lid, is what the last person out puts them back to.
passes.sustain: When you carry the last glass inside for the night, the cushions come in with you in the same trip.

the_call.title: The speckled cushion
the_call.text: You have a cushion with grey and black speckling along the piping. It got rained on, it went into the box damp, and every spring you tell yourself you will scrub it properly. Give it exactly one honest attempt: wash it with a fabric cleaner meant for outdoor material, dry it fully in sun, and put it back. If the speckling returns within the same season, the growth is inside the foam core and no surface cleaning reaches it. That cushion is finished. Replace it or go without, and either is better than a seat nobody chooses. The pattern to break is buying replacement cushions before you have fixed the reason the last set died, which was that they had nowhere dry to go in a hurry.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: Sun-aged plastic and resin chairs fail suddenly at the leg joint, and they fail under the person least able to catch themselves.

watch_for.question: Fall
watch_for.text: A folded lounger or a stacked chair left across the route between the door and the steps is the thing people trip on carrying a tray in the dark.

leave_behind.standard: One cushion per seat, all of them in the deck box overnight, and no chair blocking the door swing.
leave_behind.trigger: When you pick up the last glass at the end of an evening, the cushions ride in on the same trip.

shine_detail.shine_summary: Outdoor seating holds its grime in the joints and the fabric, not on the surfaces you can see. Hose the frames, work the grit out of the webbing, and dry every cushion on its edge so nothing goes back damp.

surfaces.surface: The chair frames and armrests
surfaces.method: Hose the whole frame first to float the loose grit off, then go over the arms and the top of the seat pan with a cloth and the neutral pH cleaner. Rinse and let the run-off carry the dirt down and away.

surfaces.surface: The woven webbing and strapping in the seat and back
surfaces.method: Grit packs into the weave and grinds the straps thin, so scrub along the bands with a stiff-bristled brush and a little soapy water, working across the weave rather than along it. Rinse until the water runs clear.

surfaces.surface: The joints where arm meets leg and the fixing bolts
surfaces.method: Brush into each joint where dirt cakes and holds moisture against the metal, then wipe the bolt heads dry with a microfiber cloth so nothing sits wet in the seam.

surfaces.surface: The hollow frame tubing
surfaces.method: Once washed, stand each chair on its side or tip it so the water trapped inside the legs runs out of the open ends instead of sitting in the tubing all summer.

surfaces.surface: The cushions and their undersides
surfaces.method: Brush off the loose debris, then sponge the fabric with a mild soapy solution and a soft cloth, blotting rather than soaking. Stand each cushion on its edge, both faces open to the air, and let it dry all the way through before it goes back.

surfaces.surface: The covers and the patch of ground behind the planters
surfaces.method: Shake the covers out, wipe them down with the neutral pH cleaner, and hang them open to dry. Sweep and mop the strip of floor behind the planters where a crumpled cover has been shedding leaf litter and holding damp.

inspect_as_you_clean: Black speckling on the underside of a cushion is mildew starting in the foam. Note which cushion and flag it before it spreads to the set.
Rust weeping from a bolt head or a weld, or an orange stain running down a leg, tells you the frame is corroding from the fixing outward.
Frayed webbing or a strap pulling loose from its rivet is the seat that will let someone through. Flag the exact chair.
Water that keeps running from a frame long after the rest has drained points to a split in the tubing holding a reservoir inside.
A cover that went away damp comes out with a musty smell and a bloom in the folds. Flag it to be washed rather than refolded.

zones.time_note: most of it in Shine, because the grease tray and burner tubes are the real work
zones.purpose: Cook over fire without leaving the grill to find a tool or wondering if there is gas.
zones.done_looks_like: Grates scraped bare, grease tray emptied and back in its rails, four tools on the grill's own hooks and no fifth anywhere, the propane tank upright with its level written on the collar, and a clear arm's length between the grill body and the siding, railing, and umbrella canopy.

passes.sort: Empty the side shelf and the cabinet under the grill. Out comes a bag of dried-out lighter cubes, three sets of tongs, a thermometer with a dead battery, and sauce bottles that spent a whole summer at outdoor temperature. Keep one long-handled tong, one spatula, one instant-read thermometer, and one basting brush.
passes.straighten: Hang the tongs and spatula on the grill's own hooks so you never walk away from a lit grill to go looking. Fuel keeps its distance from heat: the propane tank upright and outdoors, the charcoal bag sealed and off the ground, the chimney starter beside it.
passes.shine: Burn the grates off, then pull the flavorizer bars and scrape the grease tray and drip pan out into the bin rather than leaving a rendered layer to feed the next flare-up. While the burners are exposed, look up into the tubes; a spider web in a venturi tube is exactly why the flame runs yellow and lazy along one side.
passes.safety: Brush soapy water onto the propane hose and the regulator fitting, then open the valve. Bubbles mean replace the hose, not tighten it and hope. Retire any wire brush whose bristles you can pull free with your fingers, because a loose bristle ends up in food, and switch to a scraper or a coiled brush.
passes.standardize: The grease tray gets emptied on a fixed count of cooks, marked off on a card taped inside the cabinet door. A tank is written full or empty in marker on its collar the same day it changes state, so nobody has to guess by lifting it.
passes.sustain: Every time you close the lid at the end of a cook, scrape the grates while they are still hot and glance into the tray before you walk away.

the_call.title: The tank you are not sure about
the_call.text: You have two propane tanks and no idea which has gas in it, so you keep buying a third and the collection grows against the wall. Settle it with a bathroom scale. The tare weight is stamped on the collar as TW and a number; weigh the tank, subtract that number, and what remains is propane. If what is left would not carry you through one long cook with guests, that is a refill errand, not a spare. Write the answer on the collar in marker, and write it again the day a tank comes back from the exchange. While you are reading the collar, find the date stamp: tanks have a requalification life and the exchange counter will simply refuse an old one, which is worth knowing now rather than on a Saturday with people arriving. Two tanks is the right number. Anything beyond two is a storage problem pretending to be preparedness.

watch_for.question: Burn or fire
watch_for.text: Accumulated grease in the tray and drip pan is what turns a normal flare-up into a fire, and a grill within reach of siding, decking rail, or a canopy gives that fire somewhere to go.

watch_for.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
watch_for.text: Bristles shed from a worn wire brush stick to the grates and then to food, and a swallowed bristle is a genuine emergency.

watch_for.question: Burn or fire
watch_for.text: A cracked or perished propane hose leaks at the fitting, which is why the soapy water test happens before the first cook of the season and not after you smell gas.

leave_behind.standard: Four tools on the hooks, grease tray emptied on a written count of cooks, and the tank level marked on the collar.
leave_behind.trigger: When you shut the lid at the end of a cook, scrape the hot grates and look in the tray.

shine_detail.shine_summary: A grill is cleaned from the grease outward. Burn the grates, pull the trays, and get the rendered fat out to the bin before it feeds the next flare-up.

surfaces.surface: The cooking grates
surfaces.method: Run the burners hot for ten minutes to char the residue to ash, then scrape the bars clean with a grate scraper or a coiled brush rather than a wire one. Lift them out and finish with the degreaser and hot water.

surfaces.surface: The flavorizer bars and the firebox interior
surfaces.method: Pull the bars and scrape the baked-on crust off them into the bin. Scrape the loose carbon flakes off the firebox floor down toward the grease channel while everything is out.

surfaces.surface: The burner tubes and venturi openings
surfaces.method: With the bars lifted, look straight up into each burner tube and the venturi opening at the valve end, and brush any nest debris out of the mouth of the tube so the gas runs clean.

surfaces.surface: The grease tray and drip pan
surfaces.method: Slide the tray out of its rails and scrape the rendered layer into the bin, then wash both the tray and the drip pan with the food-area degreaser and hot soapy water and dry them before they go back.

surfaces.surface: The lid interior
surfaces.method: The flaking on the underside of the lid is carbonized grease, not paint, so brush it down into the firebox with a nylon brush and wipe the last film with a degreaser cloth.

surfaces.surface: The exterior body, side shelves, tool hooks, and knobs
surfaces.method: Degrease the lid and body, then go over the side shelves, the hooks, and the control knobs with the neutral pH cleaner and a microfiber cloth so no grease is left to gather dust.

surfaces.surface: The propane tank collar and the cart base
surfaces.method: Wipe the tank and its collar down with the neutral pH cleaner, then wipe the grease and grit off the cart legs and the wheels so nothing tracks grime as the grill is rolled.

surfaces.surface: The decking or pad directly under the grill
surfaces.method: Grease spatters onto the floor around a grill, so clean the pad or boards beneath it with the floor-material-compatible cleaner before the marks set and turn slick.

products_used: Grate scraper or coiled grill brush
inspect_as_you_clean: A spider web or debris blocking a venturi tube is what makes the flame run yellow and lazy along one side. If a burner cooks unevenly, flag that tube.
Rust flaking through the firebox floor, or a hole opening in it, means the base is failing where the heat and grease sit. Note where the light comes through.
Grease that has pooled past the tray and soaked into the pad or the boards is a drip path the tray is no longer catching.
A cracked or perished hose, or green corrosion crusting the regulator fitting, is worth flagging the moment you see it while wiping around the valve.
Burner ports that are rusted or clogged on one side and clear on the other explain a flame that is strong at one end and absent at the other.

zones.time_note: quick, unless the dishware decision is still open
zones.purpose: Feed people outdoors without carrying the kitchen out in four trips.
zones.done_looks_like: A bare tabletop except the umbrella and one weighted tray, six chairs tucked fully under, string lights clipped along the rail with no cord crossing the floor, and nothing stored beneath the table.

passes.sort: Clear the table down to bare surface and face what has been living on it: a citronella bucket burned to the rim, a lighter that no longer sparks, placemats gone pale on the upper side only, and the melamine plates from a barbecue two summers ago. Settle the dishware question below before anything goes back.
passes.straighten: Chairs tuck fully under the table so nobody has to sidestep a chair leg carrying a hot dish. One weighted tray holds the salt, the pepper, and the napkin weight, so laying the table is one trip out rather than four.
passes.shine: Wash the tabletop along the grain and pay attention to the collar where the umbrella pole passes through, since that ring collects grit and holds water against the table. Wipe the underside edges too, which is where hands go and where wasps like to start building.
passes.safety: An open umbrella is a sail. Match the base weight to the canopy size, crank the umbrella down whenever you leave the table, and close it before wind arrives rather than during it. Run string lights on hooks along the rail using outdoor-rated cord on a socket with a residual current device, never a household extension lead lying across boards that get wet.
passes.standardize: The table's resting state is bare except for the umbrella and the one weighted tray. Anything else arrives with a meal and leaves with it, including the candles.
passes.sustain: The last person carrying a plate inside closes the umbrella and lifts the tray on the way past.

the_call.title: Its own set, or nothing
the_call.text: Decide once whether this table gets dishware of its own, because the half-answer is what keeps it covered. Count the meals you genuinely ate out here last season. If it was more than a handful, buy one stackable set, plates, tumblers, and flatware for the number of seats, and keep it in a lidded tote in the deck box so eating outdoors costs one trip. If it was two or three meals all year, admit that, and carry the indoor plates out on those few occasions. What you must stop is the middle option: storing four faded plates, a mismatched tumbler, and a serving bowl outdoors for a set you will never complete. That orphaned half-set is precisely why the table always has something standing on it, and why it never looks ready to sit down at.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: An umbrella left open on an undersized base lifts in a gust and comes down pole first, usually across the table where people were sitting.

watch_for.question: Water and electricity
watch_for.text: Indoor extension leads run out to string lights or a speaker sit in rain and puddles on the boards, which is the one electrical shortcut outdoors that genuinely kills.

leave_behind.standard: Bare table plus umbrella and one weighted tray, umbrella cranked down whenever the table is empty.
leave_behind.trigger: Whoever carries the last plate in closes the umbrella on the way past.

shine_detail.shine_summary: Most of the work at an outdoor table is water sitting where it should be running off. Wash the top along the grain, clear the umbrella collar, and get into the shaded undersides where wasps and damp both like to settle.

surfaces.surface: The tabletop
surfaces.method: Wash along the grain with the neutral pH cleaner and a cloth, following the boards or slats rather than cutting across them, then rinse and let it sheet off the far edge.

surfaces.surface: The collar where the umbrella pole passes through the table
surfaces.method: That ring collects grit and holds a puddle against the wood, so work a detail brush around the collar, flush it clean, and dry it so no water is left standing in the joint.

surfaces.surface: The underside edges of the table
surfaces.method: Wearing gloves, run a cloth along the underside lip where hands grip to pull chairs in and where wasps begin a nest. Clear any early mud start you meet and wipe the rail clean.

surfaces.surface: The chairs, seats, backs, and rungs
surfaces.method: Wipe the seats and backs with the neutral pH cleaner, then take a detail brush to the rungs and the joints where grime rings the wood, and reach the undersides of the seats where nobody looks.

surfaces.surface: The umbrella canopy and ribs
surfaces.method: Open the canopy and brush off the bird mess and cobwebs, sponge the fabric with mild soapy water, then leave it open to dry completely before you furl it so it does not close on damp. Wipe grit out of the crank and off the ribs.

surfaces.surface: The umbrella base and pole
surfaces.method: Hose and wipe the base, and run a cloth down the pole to lift the film that builds where hands and rain both reach it.

surfaces.surface: The string lights and the rail they clip to
surfaces.method: Wipe each bulb and the cord with a barely damp cloth, never a wet one, then clean the rail behind the clips where the cord traps dirt.

surfaces.surface: The floor under and around the table
surfaces.method: Sweep or vacuum the crumbs and leaf litter from under the table and between the chair feet, then mop with the floor-material-compatible cleaner.

inspect_as_you_clean: A papery nest start or a mud tube under the table edge is a wasp or mud-dauber setting up. Flag it before it is occupied.
Canopy fabric gone thin and chalky, or stitching pulling away at the ribs, is UV rot. Note where the light shows through the weave.
Rust weeping at an umbrella rib joint, or a rib that will not sit straight, tells you the frame is seizing.
Cracked or brittle insulation on a string-light cord, or a warm or discolored connector, is worth flagging while the strand is in your hand.
Standing water that will not leave the pole collar, and a dark ring in the wood around it, means the joint is staying wet long enough to rot or rust.

zones.time_note: most of it in Sort, and the chemical shelf is the slow part
zones.purpose: Keep the containers alive and keep everything that feeds them off the ground and out of reach.
zones.done_looks_like: Every saucer empty, pots nested by size along the wall with drain holes clear, one tool caddy holding trowel, pruners, and gloves, and a latched chemical box above the tools with no more in it than you can name from the doorway.

passes.sort: Turn out every empty pot. A pot with no drainage hole and a pot still holding last year's dead root ball both go; keep the pots you will actually plant this season plus two, nested by size. Bagged potting soil that has gone solid and sour gets emptied into a bed rather than stored for a spring that will not want it.
passes.straighten: Hand tools stand in one caddy you can carry in the hand that is not holding the watering can. Long tools hang head up on a rail so no blade waits at shin height. Fertilizer and every concentrate sit above the tools, never in the row beside the watering can where a tired hand reaches.
passes.shine: Empty every saucer, then scrub the white mineral crust from the pot rims and scrape soil off the trowel and pruner blades before they go back damp. Wipe the pruner blades and put a drop of oil on the pivot while you have them open.
passes.safety: The concentrates, slug pellets, and fertilizer are the real hazard on this patio, and pellets look like food to a dog. They stay in a latched box, up high, in the container they came in, never decanted into a drink bottle or a jam jar. Empty standing water from saucers, the wheelbarrow, and the upturned pot lid after rain so mosquitoes have nowhere to breed.
passes.standardize: Every pot carries a small tag with what is in it and the month it went in, so anyone in the house can decide whether it needs water without coming to find you.
passes.sustain: When you fill the watering can, look along the row of saucers before you start pouring.

the_call.title: The half bottles
the_call.text: There is a shelf of part-used concentrates: a weed killer bought for one path, a rooting hormone, a bug spray whose label has washed to nothing. You avoid this shelf because there is no easy way to get rid of them, and pouring them down a drain is not one. Two rules settle it. First, if you cannot read the label, that container is finished, no exceptions, because an unlabelled garden chemical cannot be used safely by you or by anyone who finds it later; it goes to the household hazardous waste collection. Second, if you can read it, ask whether you have used it in the last two growing seasons. If not, it goes the same way. What survives is a short row you can name from the doorway. From this point on, buy the smallest container the shop sells rather than the best value size, because the value size is what created this shelf.

watch_for.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
watch_for.text: Slug pellets and fertilizer granules look like food to a dog, and a concentrate decanted into a drink bottle is the classic route to a poisoning in a house with children.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: A large glazed pot full of wet soil is far heavier than it looks and it lands on feet; slide it on a wheeled saucer instead of lifting it.

leave_behind.standard: Chemicals latched and labelled above the tools, every saucer empty, every pot tagged with what and when.
leave_behind.trigger: When you fill the watering can, run your eye down the saucers first.

shine_detail.shine_summary: You clean this zone so the containers keep living and nothing that feeds them ends up loose on the ground. Empty every saucer, scrub the mineral crust off the rims, and put the tools back dry.

surfaces.surface: The saucers under the pots
surfaces.method: Tip out the standing water first, then scrub the white crust and algae from the dish with a brush and the neutral pH cleaner, rinse, and dry before it goes back.

surfaces.surface: The pot rims and exteriors
surfaces.method: Scrub the chalky mineral crust off the rim and down the outside of the pot with a stiff brush and water, working the ring where salts have wept through the clay, then rinse.

surfaces.surface: The pot bases and drain holes
surfaces.method: Tip each pot and check the drain holes are open, poking a clogged one clear with a stick or a spare stake, and rinse the base where roots and grit have matted over the holes.

surfaces.surface: The wall line and shelf where the pots nest
surfaces.method: Wipe the strip of wall and the shelf the pots stand against, where damp soil has printed rings and moss has taken hold in the shade.

surfaces.surface: The trowel and pruner blades
surfaces.method: Scrape the caked soil off the trowel and the pruner blades, wipe them down, and dry them fully. Open the pruners and put a drop of tool oil on the pivot before they go back in the caddy.

surfaces.surface: The tool caddy and the watering can
surfaces.method: Tip the grit out of the bottom of the caddy and wipe it out, and rinse the watering can and its rose so nothing sits stagnant in it.

surfaces.surface: The outside of the latched chemical box
surfaces.method: Wipe the outside of the box and its latch clean. The contents stay sealed in their own containers, so this is a wipe of the box only.

surfaces.surface: The ground and footprint of the zone
surfaces.method: Sweep up the spilled compost and the crust of dried soil, then mop the floor with the floor-material-compatible cleaner so no fertilizer residue is left underfoot.

inspect_as_you_clean: A dark damp ring on the decking under a saucer that never dries out points to a saucer overflowing or a pot draining onto the boards.
Rust and pitting on a trowel or pruner blade, or a pruner spring that has lost its snap, is a tool on its way out. Note it as you dry it.
A hairline crack starting at a pot's drain hole, or a glazed pot ringing dull instead of clear, is the pot that will split with the next frost.
Wrigglers in the standing water of a saucer or the watering can are mosquito larvae, so flag any water that has been sitting long enough to breed.
A chewed corner, a leak, or a swollen container spotted inside the chemical box when you open it is a spill risk to flag, not to sort out here.

zones.time_note: most of it in Sort, once everything is out on the boards
zones.purpose: Get the cushions under a lid within a minute of the first drop of rain.
zones.done_looks_like: The lid closes flat without anyone pressing down, cushions in one layer on top, two labelled totes beneath them, and the floor of the box visible the moment the cushions come out.

passes.sort: Empty the deck box onto the boards, all of it. You will find cushions that went in damp last autumn, a croquet set missing two mallets, four covers for furniture you no longer own, and a bag of charcoal that has drawn moisture and will never light properly again. Anything that still smells of mildew after a wash does not go back in.
passes.straighten: Cushions load last and come out first, because they are the only thing in this box that has to move in a hurry. Games and covers go into flat-bottomed totes underneath, so nothing loose migrates into the corners where hands do not reach.
passes.shine: Scrub the interior and prop the lid open on a dry, breezy day until the corners are genuinely dry rather than just cool to the touch. Check that the drain holes in the base are clear, and tip the box forward to sweep out the layer of leaf mulch that has packed underneath it.
passes.safety: A deck box lid is heavy and hinged at exactly a child's hand height. Lift it and let go halfway; if it drops on its own, fit a lid stay before anything else, because crushed fingers in that hinge is the injury this zone reliably produces. Mouse droppings or shredded nesting material in stored fabric means you wash before folding, wearing gloves, and check the box for the gap they came in through.
passes.standardize: Two totes, one written games and one written covers, labelled on the short end you can read once the cushions are lifted out. The lid is the measure: if someone has to sit on it to close it, something leaves the box that day.
passes.sustain: When the cushions go in at the end of an evening, the lid gets latched, not just lowered.

the_call.title: What the box is actually for
the_call.text: You bought the deck box for cushions, and now it holds everything on this patio that has nowhere else to be. So the cushions ride on a layer of pool toys and dead covers, they never go all the way down, and the lid stands half open in the rain. Decide the box's single job and hold it against pressure: it stores cushions, because cushions are the only thing out here that must be under a lid within a minute of the first drop. Everything else that has crept in gets a real home in the garage or leaves the property this weekend. Carrying it all out will look like waste while you are doing it. It is not. A box that cannot close protects nothing inside it, so the arrangement you have now is already costing you the cushions, one damp night at a time.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: An unsupported deck box lid falls at hand height and catches fingers on the hinge side, which is where children reach when they help.

watch_for.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
watch_for.text: Mice nest in stored cushions and fabric, and shaking out contaminated bedding indoors sends droppings and dust into the air you breathe.

leave_behind.standard: Cushions only on top, two labelled totes below, lid closing flat with no pressure.
leave_behind.trigger: When the cushions go in for the night, the latch goes across.

shine_detail.shine_summary: The whole point of a deck box is a dry lid closing over dry cushions. Scrub it out, air it until the corners are genuinely dry, and clear the drains before anything soft goes back in.

surfaces.surface: The lid exterior
surfaces.method: Wipe the top of the lid down with the neutral pH cleaner and a microfiber cloth, clearing the leaf litter and pollen that cakes on and washes into the seam in rain.

surfaces.surface: The lid underside and the hinge
surfaces.method: Wipe the inside face of the lid, then brush the grit and cobweb out of the hinge line so nothing gums up the pivot.

surfaces.surface: The sealing edge and the interior walls
surfaces.method: Empty the box completely, wipe the rubber sealing edge in its fold, then scrub the interior walls with warm soapy water and rinse.

surfaces.surface: The box floor and the drain holes
surfaces.method: Scrub the floor of the box once the walls are done, and check that the drain holes in the base are open, poking any that are blocked clear so water has a way out.

surfaces.surface: The interior, aired dry
surfaces.method: Prop the lid open on a dry, breezy day and leave it until the corners are genuinely dry to the touch, not just cool, before anything soft returns.

surfaces.surface: The totes and the cushions stored inside
surfaces.method: Wipe the outside of the labelled totes and confirm the labels still read, then brush the cushions and air them alongside the open box.

surfaces.surface: The ground under the box
surfaces.method: Tip the box forward and sweep out the packed layer of leaf mulch that has built up underneath it, then mop the footprint with the floor-material-compatible cleaner.

surfaces.surface: The latch and handles
surfaces.method: Wipe the latch and the carry handles clean so the closure still seats properly and nothing grinds when the lid drops.

inspect_as_you_clean: Mouse droppings or shredded nesting material in the fabric or the totes tells you the box has a resident. Flag it before you handle the contents.
A gnaw hole or a gap at a corner joint is how they got in. Note where the light shows through the seam.
A musty smell or a corner that stays damp after airing means the box is not sealing or not draining as it should.
Black mildew spotting spreading up the interior walls is moisture that has been trapped inside long enough to bloom.
A pool that will not leave the base points to drain holes that are blocked rather than doing their job.

zones.time_note: most of it in Shine, because raking the board gaps is slow and it is also the inspection
zones.purpose: The structure you stand on and lean against, kept sound and kept clear.
zones.done_looks_like: Nothing on the deck that is not furniture, daylight visible through the gaps between boards, no green film on the shaded treads, and every rail post immovable when you push it hard.

passes.sort: This zone earns its state by having nothing stored in it. The planter that has drifted into the walking route, the hose coiled across the top step, and the bag of paving sand leaning on a rail post all come off the deck entirely, because each of them holds damp against the wood it sits on as well as standing in your way.
passes.straighten: Walk the route from the door to the steps to the gate carrying a full laundry basket in both arms so you cannot see your feet. Whatever you have to step around gets moved. The mat sits square at the threshold with its edges lying flat, not curling up at a corner.
passes.shine: Rake the gaps between boards clear with a putty knife or a paint stirrer, because a blocked gap holds water against the board ends and that is precisely where rot begins. Then scrub the green algae film off the shaded boards and the stair treads, which is the slipperiest surface anywhere on the property after rain.
passes.safety: Grab the top rail at every post and push hard, outward and then down. Any movement, any softness under your thumb, any screw head standing proud is a stop and fix today. Check that every stair tread rises the same height as the ones above and below it, and that the step lights still come on, because one odd riser in the dark is how people go down. Find it, and fix it now.
passes.standardize: A dated tag inside the back door records when the rail was last pushed and the boards last probed, so the next check starts from a written date rather than an argument about whether you did it in spring.
passes.sustain: Every time you sweep the deck, push the rail at two posts before the broom goes away.

the_call.title: The board that gives
the_call.text: There is a board you step over without thinking, or one that flexes slightly under your weight, and you have quietly filed it as fine. Test it properly instead. Push a screwdriver into the board where it crosses a joist, and again into the board end nearest the house. If the tip sinks in with light pressure, that board is finished and replacing one board is a morning's work. The harder judgment is what a soft board is telling you. If two boards side by side are soft, or if the softness is at the ledger where the deck meets the wall of the house, then the framing underneath has the problem and the surface is only the symptom. The rule that settles it: soft in one spot on top, replace the board yourself; soft in two adjacent places or soft at the wall, stop putting people on it and get someone underneath it with a torch before the next time you have guests standing out here together.

watch_for.question: Fall
watch_for.text: A railing post that moves when you push it will not hold an adult who stumbles into it, and the drop off the side of a deck is onto whatever is stored below.

watch_for.question: Fall
watch_for.text: Algae film on the shaded boards and the stair treads turns to grease after rain, and the treads are where a slip costs the most.

watch_for.question: Fall, cut, or crush
watch_for.text: Popped fasteners and lifted splinters on a deck people cross barefoot in summer cut feet, and a raised screw head is also what catches a toe.

leave_behind.standard: Nothing stored on the walking route, gaps clear, and a dated tag recording the last rail push and board probe.
leave_behind.trigger: Every time you sweep, push the rail at two posts before you put the broom away.

shine_detail.shine_summary: This is the surface you trust with your whole weight, so cleaning it is how you read it. Rake the gaps clear, scrub the algae off the shaded treads, and let the deck tell you where water has been sitting.

surfaces.surface: The deck board surface
surfaces.method: Sweep the whole deck first, then scrub the boards with a deck brush and the neutral pH cleaner, working with the grain, and rinse the loosened dirt off toward the edge.

surfaces.surface: The gaps between the boards
surfaces.method: Rake each gap clear with a putty knife or a paint stirrer until you can see daylight through it, because a packed gap holds water against the board ends and that is where rot begins.

surfaces.surface: The board ends and the house-side junction
surfaces.method: Brush the debris out of the line where the boards meet the house wall or the ledger, the trap that collects the most leaf litter and stays wettest.

surfaces.surface: The stair treads and risers
surfaces.method: Scrub the green algae film off the treads with a stiff brush, since that shaded film is the slipperiest surface on the property after rain, then wipe down the risers and the stringers beside them.

surfaces.surface: The top rail and the balusters
surfaces.method: Wash the top rail where hands leave grime, then go down the balusters and into the gaps between the spindles where dirt and cobwebs gather out of sight.

surfaces.surface: The rail posts and their bases
surfaces.method: Brush the grit out of the joint where each post meets the deck and wipe the base plate, clearing the spot where standing debris keeps the fixing wet.

surfaces.surface: The step lights and lenses
surfaces.method: Wipe each step-light lens with a barely damp cloth and dry it right away, so no water sits in the fixture and the light still reaches the tread it is meant to show.

surfaces.surface: The area under the deck
surfaces.method: Sweep out whatever has drifted or been stored beneath the deck so the space stays clear and the underside of the boards can breathe and dry.

inspect_as_you_clean: A board end or a blocked gap that stays dark and spongy under the brush is rot setting in. Press it and flag any board that gives.
Rust bleeding out of a fastener and staining the board around it means the screw or nail is corroding below the surface.
A proud screw head or a lifted splinter that catches the brush is a bare foot waiting to happen. Note exactly where it sits.
A tread that flexes underfoot as you scrub, or a stringer gone soft at the bottom, is a stair losing its footing.
A step light gone dead or fogged behind its lens, and algae that regrows fast in one spot, both point to water pooling where it should drain.
